projectTitle: Everpeak Software: The Churn Score That Looked Too Good to Be True
projectTagline: A 20-video, start-to-finish data science build for a fictional B2B SaaS company -- a real 90-day churn risk model taken from SQL Server extraction through scikit-learn and LightGBM, deployed to Azure ML, and corrected after a genuine target-leakage bug is found in production, not glossed over.
businessContext: Everpeak Software is a B2B project-management SaaS company with about 40,000 paying customer accounts on annual contracts. Customer Success and Sales have no early-warning signal for churn today -- they find out an account is at risk only after it has already sent a non-renewal notice. Dana Okafor (VP of Customer Success) and Tom Bellamy (Head of Renewals) need a risk score early enough to actually act on, built from the real SQL Server data Renata Silva's team owns. Felix Granger (Head of Data Science) and Grace Lindqvist (ML Engineer) build and deploy it -- and have to find and fix a real target-leakage bug when the model's offline performance turns out not to match reality in production.
architectureSummary: SQL Server (`EVERPEAK_PROD`) as the source of truth across Accounts, Subscriptions, UsageEvents, SupportTickets, and Invoices; Python/pandas for extraction and feature engineering; scikit-learn Logistic Regression as the baseline and LightGBM as the production model; SHAP for explainability; a weekly Azure ML Batch Endpoint for deployment (not real-time, to match the business's actual weekly renewals cadence), scoring every active account and writing results to `dbo.ChurnRiskScores`. A genuine target-leakage bug in two trailing-window features is found through a time-consistent backtest and fixed by anchoring every windowed feature to a single fixed observation date per training row.

lessons.title: Meeting Everpeak: Why Churn Is Invisible Until It's Too Late
lessons.summary: The discovery meeting: Customer Success only learns an account is at risk when it sends a non-renewal notice, and what you have to learn about Everpeak's real data before you can design anything to fix that.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Over the next 20 videos, you'll walk through one complete, start-to-finish data science engagement for a fictional B2B project-management SaaS company, **Everpeak Software** -- roughly 40,000 paying customer accounts, each on an annual contract that has to be renewed every twelve months. Everpeak's revenue is almost entirely recurring: when an account renews, that revenue continues; when it doesn't, it's gone. Right now, the first signal anyone at Everpeak gets that an account is in trouble is the non-renewal notice itself -- the account's own written word that they're leaving. By then there is nothing left to do.

This video starts exactly where this kind of project always has to start: not with a model, not with a line of Python, but with a meeting where you find out precisely what the business problem is, who feels it, and where the real data actually lives. You, Felix Granger, are Everpeak's Head of Data Science. **Dana Okafor**, VP of Customer Success, is the business sponsor who called this meeting -- she wants an early-warning signal her team can act on before an account is already gone. **Renata Silva**, Everpeak's Data/Analytics Engineer, owns and knows the real source of truth: the live SQL Server database **`EVERPEAK_PROD`**, the same OLTP tables the product itself runs on. **Tom Bellamy**, Head of Renewals/Sales, is the eventual end consumer of whatever this project produces -- his team is the one who would actually act on a risk score. By the end of this series, Everpeak has a weekly risk score, built and evaluated honestly, deployed to production, and in Tom's team's hands. This lesson is step one: understanding the problem and the data before touching either.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a yearly membership to a neighborhood pool. Every summer, families decide whether to renew for next year. Right now, the pool's front desk only finds out a family isn't coming back when that family mails in a letter saying "we're not renewing." By the time that letter arrives, the family has already made up their mind -- there's nothing left to say to change it.

That's exactly Everpeak's problem, except instead of a pool membership, it's software that 40,000 companies pay for every year. Dana Okafor's team wants to know *before* the "we're leaving" letter shows up -- while there's still time to call the family and ask what's wrong, or fix whatever's bothering them. But right now, nobody has a way to guess which families are quietly unhappy before they write that letter. Your job starts with figuring out what clues might already exist -- in records of who's been swimming less, who's complained to the lifeguard, who's behind on dues -- that could have hinted at the decision before the letter ever got written.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The detail that matters most in this discovery meeting isn't the headline -- "we only find out when they tell us" -- it's the specific absence of any leading indicator anywhere in Everpeak's current workflow. Non-renewal is a lagging signal by definition: it's the outcome, not a precursor to it. A real early-warning system has to be built from behavioral and transactional signals that exist *before* that outcome, which means this project lives or dies on whether Everpeak's existing OLTP data actually contains those precursors, and whether they're accessible without standing up a data warehouse first.

That's why the second half of this meeting belongs to Renata Silva, not Dana. Dana can tell you the business pain; only Renata can tell you what's actually queryable. Everpeak has no data warehouse and no dedicated analytics layer -- the source of truth is the live production database, `EVERPEAK_PROD`, the same SQL Server instance the application itself reads and writes against. Five tables matter here: `dbo.Accounts` (the account master record, including `ContractRenewalDate` and the nullable `ChurnDate`), `dbo.Subscriptions` (billing-level `MonthlyRevenue` and `PlanTier` history), `dbo.UsageEvents` (raw login and feature-use events, one row per event), `dbo.SupportTickets` (opened/closed tickets with a `Severity`), and `dbo.Invoices` (billing cycles, with `DaysLate` as a direct signal of account health). Every one of those is a live, growing OLTP table, not a curated analytics table -- which means this project's first real engineering decision, still a lesson or two away, is how to query production responsibly without becoming a performance problem for the application itself.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Walk in already knowing what you don't know

Before the meeting, write down what you'd need to confirm, not just what you expect to hear:

- Is "non-renewal" the only signal CS currently has, or are there informal signals (a CSM's gut feeling, a slipping NPS score) that never get written down anywhere queryable?
- Does Everpeak have a data warehouse, or is production SQL Server the only place this data lives?
- Who owns that data day to day, and who actually knows its quirks?

## Step 2 -- Run the meeting and get the real problem in Dana's own words

```
DANA:   By the time an account sends us a non-renewal notice, the
        decision is already made. My team has no signal before that --
        no dashboard, no score, nothing. We find out we lost an
        account the same moment we lose it. I want something that
        flags an account as at-risk while there's still time to call
        them.

FELIX:  When you say "at risk," what have CSMs told you they notice,
        even informally, before an account leaves?

DANA:   Logins drop off. Tickets pile up and don't get resolved fast.
        Sometimes invoices start going out late and staying unpaid
        longer. But none of that is tracked anywhere we can act on --
        it's just what a sharp CSM happens to remember about their own
        accounts.
```

## Step 3 -- Bring in Renata and get the real data landscape, not the assumed one

```
FELIX:   Where does all of that actually live?

RENATA:  One SQL Server database, EVERPEAK_PROD. No warehouse, no
         analytics replica -- it's the live OLTP database the app
         itself runs on. Five tables will matter most to you:

         dbo.Accounts        (AccountId, CompanyName, Industry,
                              SeatCount, ContractStartDate,
                              ContractRenewalDate, ChurnDate,
                              PlanTier)
         dbo.Subscriptions   (SubscriptionId, AccountId,
                              MonthlyRevenue, PlanTier, StartDate,
                              EndDate)
         dbo.UsageEvents     (EventId, AccountId, UserId, EventType,
                              EventTimestamp)
         dbo.SupportTickets  (TicketId, AccountId, OpenedDate,
                              ClosedDate, Severity)
         dbo.Invoices        (InvoiceId, AccountId, InvoiceDate,
                              AmountDue, PaidDate, DaysLate)

         ChurnDate on Accounts is NULL for every account still active.
         UsageEvents is enormous and append-only -- millions of rows,
         growing every day. Nothing here was built for analytics; it
         was built to run the product.

FELIX:   So anything we query against this has to respect that it's
         live and production-critical.

RENATA:  Exactly. Whatever you build, I want to review the queries
         before they run against anything but a replica or an
         off-peak window.
```

## Step 4 -- Write the discovery summary while it's fresh

```
EVERPEAK SOFTWARE -- DISCOVERY SUMMARY

Business problem:   Customer Success has no warning signal before an
                     account sends a non-renewal notice; by then the
                     decision is already made.
Sponsor:             Dana Okafor, VP Customer Success.
Informal signals CS already trusts: falling logins, unresolved
  support tickets, late invoices -- currently untracked and unscored.
System of record:   EVERPEAK_PROD (SQL Server), live OLTP, owned by
                     Renata Silva. No data warehouse exists.
Key tables:          dbo.Accounts, dbo.Subscriptions, dbo.UsageEvents,
                     dbo.SupportTickets, dbo.Invoices.
Constraint:          Any querying must not degrade production; Renata
                     reviews query plans before they run against
                     EVERPEAK_PROD outside a replica or off-peak window.
```

## Step 5 -- Confirm it in writing with Dana and Renata

Send this summary to both and ask directly: "Did I capture this accurately?" Every requirement you write in the next lesson traces back to a line in this document -- and Renata's sign-off on the data landscape is what keeps the next lesson's requirement honest about what's actually queryable.

Any extraction work has to go through her review before it touches anything but a replica or an off-peak window.

This project is about turning that existing data into a warning we can act on before the decision is final.

lessons.title: Turning 'Stop the Churn' Into a Testable Requirement
lessons.summary: Converting Dana's 'give us a warning sign' into one precise, testable requirement: a 90-day-ahead risk score per account, defined against an exact OBSERVATION_DATE snapshot, refreshed on a cadence Tom Bellamy's team can actually act on.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Discovery gave you a real problem and an honest picture of Everpeak's data -- but "give us a warning sign" and "stop the churn" aren't requirements yet, they're intentions. This lesson turns them into something you can actually design and later test against: a risk score computed per account, as of a specific snapshot in time, that predicts whether the account will churn within a fixed, actionable window.

That window has to be long enough for Tom Bellamy's Renewals/Sales team to actually do something with it -- a risk score delivered the week before a renewal decision is already made is no better than the non-renewal notice itself. This lesson fixes the exact prediction target this entire series builds toward: given a snapshot date called `OBSERVATION_DATE`, predict whether the account's `ChurnDate` falls strictly after `OBSERVATION_DATE` and within `OBSERVATION_DATE + 90 days`. Every later lesson -- the feature pipeline, the model, the evaluation, the deployment -- answers to this one definition.
lessons.explainSimple:
Remember the pool membership? After everyone agrees they want a warning sign, somebody still has to answer: a warning sign of *what*, exactly, and *how far ahead*? "Warn us if a family might not renew" doesn't tell the front desk anything useful by itself. Does it mean warn them the day before the letter arrives, which is useless? Or three months before, while there's still time to call and ask how the family's doing?

That's what this lesson nails down for Everpeak. Instead of "warn us about churn," the real rule becomes: as of today, for every single account, is there a good chance they'll leave sometime in the next 90 days? Ninety days is picked on purpose -- it's enough time for Tom's team to actually pick up the phone and do something, instead of finding out the week before the contract runs out.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A requirement that can't be falsified isn't a requirement, it's a hope -- and "give CS a warning sign" is exactly that until it's pinned to a precise label definition and a precise time window. The window itself is a business decision, not a modeling one: it has to be long enough that Tom Bellamy's team can realistically intervene before a renewal decision is finalized, which both Dana and Tom agree is roughly 90 days out from any given day.

That gives this project's prediction target its exact shape: for a given snapshot date, `OBSERVATION_DATE`, the label is 1 if the account's `ChurnDate` (from `dbo.Accounts`) falls strictly after `OBSERVATION_DATE` and within `OBSERVATION_DATE + 90 days`, and 0 if the account remains active through that entire 90-day window. An account that has already churned as of `OBSERVATION_DATE` is excluded from that row entirely -- it isn't a valid snapshot for that account, because there's nothing left to predict. This framing matters because it's what makes a training set buildable at all: every historical row is really a (account, `OBSERVATION_DATE`) pair, not just an account, which means the same account can contribute multiple rows at different points in its history, each one a fair test of "would this account have looked risky from here." Getting this exactly right now is what keeps every later feature-engineering decision honest -- a feature computed with information from *after* `OBSERVATION_DATE` would leak the answer into the question, which is exactly the kind of mistake this definition exists to prevent.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Pull the real constraint out of Tom's side of the business

```
FELIX:  Dana, you want a warning sign. How far ahead does it actually
        need to be for Tom's team to use it?

DANA:   Tom, you're the one who'd act on it.

TOM:    Renewal conversations really start in earnest about three
        months out. If I get a flag the week before the contract
        expires, it's too late -- the account's already decided. I
        need it with enough runway to actually schedule a call,
        understand what's wrong, and maybe loop in their CSM.

FELIX:  So the useful window is roughly 90 days ahead of a renewal
        decision, not 90 days ahead of the renewal date itself.

TOM:    Right -- as early as you can give it to me, as long as it's
        reliable.
```

## Step 2 -- Fix the exact prediction target in writing

This is the definition every later lesson in this series refers back to, so write it precisely, not approximately:

```
PREDICTION TARGET -- EVERPEAK CHURN RISK (V1)

Given a snapshot date, OBSERVATION_DATE, for a given account:

  Label = 1  if ChurnDate is NOT NULL
             AND ChurnDate > OBSERVATION_DATE
             AND ChurnDate <= OBSERVATION_DATE + 90 days

  Label = 0  if the account is still active
             (ChurnDate IS NULL, or ChurnDate falls after
              OBSERVATION_DATE + 90 days)

  Excluded:  any account where ChurnDate <= OBSERVATION_DATE --
             the account had already churned as of the snapshot,
             so this is not a valid row for that OBSERVATION_DATE.
```

## Step 3 -- Sanity-check the definition against real rows in EVERPEAK_PROD

Before trusting this definition, run it against a sample and read the output by hand:

```sql
-- Sanity check: what would the label look like for a sample
-- OBSERVATION_DATE, using dbo.Accounts as it exists today?
DECLARE @OBSERVATION_DATE DATE = '2026-01-15';

SELECT
    AccountId,
    CompanyName,
    ChurnDate,
    CASE
        WHEN ChurnDate IS NULL THEN 'ACTIVE (label=0)'
        WHEN ChurnDate <= @OBSERVATION_DATE THEN 'EXCLUDE (already churned)'
        WHEN ChurnDate <= DATEADD(day, 90, @OBSERVATION_DATE) THEN 'AT-RISK (label=1)'
        ELSE 'ACTIVE (label=0)'
    END AS label_status
FROM dbo.Accounts
ORDER BY ChurnDate;
```

Walk a handful of rows from each bucket past Renata -- she'll know immediately if `ChurnDate` is ever backfilled late or recorded inconsistently, which would quietly break this definition.

## Step 4 -- Agree on the refresh cadence

```
DANA:   How often would this actually update?

FELIX:  Weekly is the plan -- every account gets a fresh score once a
        week, using the latest OBSERVATION_DATE as of that run. Daily
        would be more responsive but isn't justified yet: usage and
        billing behavior that signals risk doesn't meaningfully shift
        inside a single day, and a weekly cadence is far cheaper to
        run and to monitor.

TOM:    Weekly works. I'm not checking this daily anyway.
```

## Step 5 -- Write the requirement and get it signed off

```
EVERPEAK -- V1 AVAILABILITY/TIMING REQUIREMENT

REQ-1: Every paying account receives a churn-risk score, refreshed
       weekly, predicting churn within the next 90 days as of that
       week's OBSERVATION_DATE (see exact label definition above).
REQ-2: The score must reach Tom Bellamy's team with enough lead time
       to act before a renewal decision is finalized -- the 90-day
       window is chosen specifically to cover that.
REQ-3: Already-churned accounts are excluded from scoring, not
       scored as "high risk" -- there is nothing left to act on.
```

Save this as `Everpeak_V1_Prediction_Target_v1.md` alongside the Lesson 1 discovery summary. Get explicit sign-off from Dana and Tom on the 90-day window specifically -- that's the number the whole series is built around.

Confirmed with Renata that ChurnDate in dbo.Accounts is reliable enough to sanity-check this against real rows before building any feature pipeline on top of it.

lessons.title: Scoping V1: A Risk Score, Not a Fix
lessons.summary: Drawing a hard line around what V1 actually ships -- a risk score, an explanation of why, and who sees it -- and naming what's explicitly deferred: automated outreach and any fix to the product problems that cause churn in the first place.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
You now have a precise, signed-off prediction target. Before any feature gets engineered or any model gets trained, this lesson draws a hard written line around what V1 of this engagement actually delivers -- and, just as importantly, what it explicitly does not. For Everpeak, V1 ships exactly three things: a churn-risk score per account, refreshed weekly; an explanation of *why* that account was flagged, so Tom Bellamy's team isn't acting on a mystery number; and a defined audience -- Tom's Renewals/Sales team, with Dana Okafor's Customer Success org as a secondary consumer -- who actually sees the score and the explanation.

What's explicitly out of scope for V1, named in writing rather than left to assumption, is anything that acts on the score automatically -- no auto-triggered retention emails, no automatic discounting, no workflow that contacts a customer without a human deciding to -- and anything that fixes the underlying product problems the score might reveal. If accounts are churning because a feature is broken or a competitor is cheaper, this project will surface that pattern; it will not attempt to fix the product. Those are real, valuable follow-on efforts, and naming them now as deferred -- not ignored -- is what keeps this project from quietly growing into three different projects before it's shipped one.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a smoke detector. A good smoke detector does exactly one job really well: it notices smoke and makes a loud noise so people know something's wrong, right now, while there's still time to do something about it. A smoke detector that also tried to put out the fire, call the fire department, and rebuild the kitchen afterward would be a much worse smoke detector -- it would be slower, more likely to break, and harder to trust for the one job that actually matters.

This project is Everpeak's smoke detector for churn. It notices which accounts smell like trouble and says so loudly and clearly, with a reason attached. It does not call the customer, it does not offer them a discount on its own, and it definitely does not go fix whatever is actually wrong with the product. Those are real jobs for real people to do next -- the detector's job is just to make sure they find out in time to do them.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Scope discipline matters here specifically because a churn-risk score is an unusually tempting thing to over-promise on. The moment a working score exists, it's natural for stakeholders to ask "can it also just email the at-risk accounts a discount automatically?" or "can this tell us what to fix in the product?" Both are reasonable questions and both are real future work -- and both would, if bundled into V1, turn a well-scoped scoring and explanation system into an open-ended automation and product-strategy project with no clear finish line.

The deferral has to be specific and honest, not a vague "later." Automated retention outreach is deferred because triggering customer-facing action without a human decision carries real risk -- a false positive contacting a healthy account with a retention offer is a different, and arguably worse, failure mode than a missed true positive, and nobody has designed or tested for that risk yet. Root-cause product fixes are deferred because they're a different kind of work entirely: SHAP-based explanations (covered later in this series) can surface that, say, accounts with falling `UsageEvents` and high `SupportTickets` severity tend to churn, but turning that into an actual product fix is Product and Engineering's job, informed by this project's output, not a deliverable of this project itself. What V1 commits to is narrower and fully ownable: a number, a reason, and a defined set of eyes on both -- Tom Bellamy's team to act on the renewal conversation, Dana Okafor's team as the secondary audience who also needs visibility into accounts they're responsible for.

lessons.title: Choosing the Stack: SQL Server, Python, and Azure ML
lessons.summary: The first real architecture decision: SQL Server for extraction, pandas for wrangling, scikit-learn for a Logistic Regression baseline, LightGBM for the improved model, SHAP for explainability, and an Azure ML Batch Endpoint writing to dbo.ChurnRiskScores -- justified against real alternatives for this company's real constraints.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With scope locked, this is the first real architecture decision: exactly what tools build and run the weekly churn-risk score, end to end. The stack this series uses, and justifies in this lesson, is: **SQL Server** (T-SQL) for extracting from `EVERPEAK_PROD`; **Python with pandas** for wrangling that extract into a modeling-ready table; **scikit-learn**'s Logistic Regression as the first, simplest baseline model; **LightGBM** as the improved, production-bound model once the baseline exists; **SHAP** for the per-account, per-feature explanations Lesson 3 committed to shipping; and **Azure Machine Learning**, specifically an **Azure ML Batch Endpoint** -- a scheduled, weekly batch scoring job, not a real-time or online API -- for deployment, with every run's output landing in a new table, **`dbo.ChurnRiskScores`**, that Tom Bellamy's team queries directly.

Each piece of this stack earns its place against a real alternative, not just convention. Batch beats real-time because renewal decisions aren't made minute-to-minute -- a weekly refresh matches how the business actually consumes the score, at a fraction of the operational cost and complexity of a live endpoint. LightGBM beats a deep-learning approach because the data here is entirely tabular -- account, subscription, usage, ticket, and invoice records, not images or raw text -- and because SHAP's explanations, which this project is contractually committed to delivering, are both faster to compute and easier for Grace Lindqvist to maintain in production against a gradient-boosted tree model than against a neural network.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you're planning a school bake sale. You wouldn't rent a professional commercial kitchen with a full-time chef on call twenty-four hours a day just to bake cookies once a week for a Saturday sale -- that's way more than the job needs, and way more expensive to keep running. You'd use a regular kitchen, bake once a week on a schedule, and have a simple, honest recipe card that anyone can read and understand, rather than a secret recipe nobody -- including you -- can explain.

That's exactly the thinking behind Everpeak's tools. The risk score only needs to be freshly baked once a week, not every single second, so there's no need for an expensive "always-on" kitchen -- a scheduled batch job on a calendar is enough. And the recipe itself should be one Tom Bellamy's team can actually understand the reasons behind, not a mysterious black box nobody can explain when someone asks "why is this account flagged?"
lessons.explainProfessional:
Every choice in this stack traces back to a real constraint from the first three lessons, not a default. Start with deployment shape: Lesson 2 fixed the refresh cadence at weekly, which means a real-time, always-on scoring API is solving a problem Everpeak doesn't have. An **Azure ML Batch Endpoint** -- triggered on a schedule, scoring every active account in one run, writing results to `dbo.ChurnRiskScores` -- matches the actual consumption pattern at a fraction of the infrastructure cost and operational surface area of a managed real-time endpoint that would sit mostly idle between weekly business decisions. A real-time endpoint earns its complexity when predictions are needed on-demand, mid-transaction; nothing here is on-demand.

Model choice follows the same logic. The source data is entirely structured and tabular -- `dbo.Accounts`, `dbo.Subscriptions`, `dbo.UsageEvents`, `dbo.SupportTickets`, `dbo.Invoices` -- with no images, free text, or sequential/temporal signal rich enough to justify a deep-learning architecture. Gradient-boosted trees, specifically **LightGBM**, are the well-established strong default for tabular problems like this one: they handle mixed numeric and categorical features natively, tolerate missing values gracefully, and train fast enough to iterate quickly during development. Critically, they also pair cleanly with **SHAP**, whose tree-based explainer is both exact and fast against gradient-boosted trees -- a meaningfully easier path to the per-account explanation Lesson 3 scoped as a V1 deliverable than extracting comparable explanations from a neural network would be. **scikit-learn**'s Logistic Regression earns its place first, not as a discard: a simple, fully interpretable linear baseline is what later proves LightGBM's added complexity is actually worth it, rather than assuming a fancier model is automatically better. None of this stack choice says anything yet about how well the resulting model actually performs -- that's a question this series answers honestly once there's a real baseline and real evaluation to look at, not one to guess at here.

lessons.title: Designing the Feature Pipeline Around What We'd Actually Know
lessons.summary: Mapping every candidate feature back to dbo.Accounts, dbo.Subscriptions, dbo.UsageEvents, dbo.SupportTickets, and dbo.Invoices, under one rule: a feature only earns a place in the model if it's something we'd genuinely know as of the day we're predicting.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
The last few lessons settled the business problem and the tech stack. This lesson is where that stack gets pointed at `EVERPEAK_PROD` and turned into an actual feature list -- the columns the Logistic Regression baseline and the LightGBM model will eventually learn from. Felix sits down with Renata Silva, who knows exactly what lives in each of the five source tables, and the two of them sort candidate signals into three groups: account and plan characteristics from `dbo.Accounts` and `dbo.Subscriptions` (seat count, plan tier, monthly revenue, how long the account has been a customer), behavioral signals from `dbo.UsageEvents` (how actively people at the account are logging in and using the product), and support/billing signals from `dbo.SupportTickets` and `dbo.Invoices` (open tickets, late payments).

The guiding principle Felix states out loud in the planning doc, and that the whole pipeline is designed around, is simple to say and surprisingly easy to get subtly wrong in practice: every feature has to be something the model would actually have access to on the real day it's asked to score an account, not something that's only knowable in hindsight. This lesson is the design of that pipeline -- which features, from which tables, computed how -- before any of it gets built in pandas.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you're trying to predict, from clues available right now, whether a plant is going to wilt in the next couple weeks -- how much you've been watering it, how much sun it gets, whether its leaves already look a little droopy today. Those are fair clues. What wouldn't be fair is using a clue like "how much water did it get the week it actually died" -- because on the day you're making your prediction, that week hasn't happened yet. You can't peek at the future and call it a clue.

That's the whole job in this lesson: Felix and Renata go through every number sitting in Everpeak's database -- how many times people logged in recently, how many support tickets are open, how late the last invoice payment was -- and ask, for each one, "would we actually have this number in hand on the day we're trying to predict?" The ones that pass that test go into the feature list. The database has five big tables full of real customer activity, and this lesson decides exactly which pieces of each one become inputs to the model.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This lesson produces the feature specification that the pandas wrangling step (a later lesson) will implement verbatim. Three feature families come out of it. Account and subscription features are static or slow-moving snapshot values: `SeatCount`, `PlanTier`, `MonthlyRevenue` (from `dbo.Subscriptions`), and tenure, derived as the gap between `ContractStartDate` and the snapshot date. These carry no temporal-window risk -- they're simple point-in-time lookups.

The behavioral family is where the real design work happens. `dbo.UsageEvents` logs every login and feature-use event with an `EventTimestamp`, so the natural features are trailing-window counts: `logins_last_30d`, `logins_last_90d`, and `days_since_last_login`. The design decision Felix and Renata land on is to anchor each account's window to its own most relevant reference point -- for an account that has already churned, that's its `ChurnDate` (there's no reason to count logins an account racked up after it had already left), and for an account still active, that's the day the extract is pulled. In SQL terms, that's a window bounded by `COALESCE(ChurnDate, CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE))` for every account, rather than one single date applied uniformly:

```sql
SELECT
    a.AccountId,
    COUNT(ue.EventId) AS logins_last_30d
FROM dbo.Accounts a
LEFT JOIN dbo.UsageEvents ue
    ON ue.AccountId = a.AccountId
   AND ue.EventType = 'Login'
   AND ue.EventTimestamp >= DATEADD(DAY, -30, COALESCE(a.ChurnDate, CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE)))
   AND ue.EventTimestamp <  COALESCE(a.ChurnDate, CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE))
GROUP BY a.AccountId;
```

`days_since_last_login` follows the same anchoring logic. The support/billing family is similar in shape: `open_support_tickets_last_90d` from `dbo.SupportTickets` (same trailing-window pattern), and a billing-health signal built from `dbo.Invoices.DaysLate` on the most recent invoice. All of it gets written up as a feature spec Renata signs off on before a line of extraction code gets written.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Lay out the three feature families

Felix and Renata start with a whiteboard split into three columns, one per source-table family, and populate it with every column that could plausibly carry signal:

| Family | Source tables | Candidate features |
|---|---|---|
| Account & plan | `dbo.Accounts`, `dbo.Subscriptions` | `SeatCount`, `PlanTier`, `MonthlyRevenue`, tenure (`ContractStartDate` to snapshot date) |
| Behavioral (usage) | `dbo.UsageEvents` | `logins_last_30d`, `logins_last_90d`, `days_since_last_login` |
| Support & billing | `dbo.SupportTickets`, `dbo.Invoices` | `open_support_tickets_last_90d`, most recent `DaysLate` |

## Step 2 -- Define the account & plan features

These are the easy ones. `SeatCount` and `PlanTier` come straight off `dbo.Accounts`. `MonthlyRevenue` comes off the account's current row in `dbo.Subscriptions` (filtered to the subscription with no `EndDate`, or the latest `StartDate` if more than one is open). Tenure is a date subtraction: snapshot date minus `ContractStartDate`, in days. None of these need a trailing window -- they describe the account as it stands right now, not a rate of activity over time.

## Step 3 -- Define the behavioral features and their time windows

`dbo.UsageEvents` is the richest table in `EVERPEAK_PROD` -- every login and feature-use action, with an `EventTimestamp`. Three features come out of it: `logins_last_30d`, `logins_last_90d`, and `days_since_last_login`.

The design question that matters most here is: a window of 30 or 90 days *back from what date*? Felix and Renata's answer is to anchor each account's window to the date most relevant to that account's own story -- `ChurnDate` for an account that already left (so the window doesn't run past the point it stopped being a customer), and the extract date for an account still active:

```sql
DECLARE @anchor DATE = COALESCE(a.ChurnDate, CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE));

SELECT a.AccountId,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN ue.EventTimestamp >= DATEADD(DAY, -30, @anchor) THEN 1 END) AS logins_last_30d,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN ue.EventTimestamp >= DATEADD(DAY, -90, @anchor) THEN 1 END) AS logins_last_90d,
       DATEDIFF(DAY, MAX(ue.EventTimestamp), @anchor) AS days_since_last_login
FROM dbo.Accounts a
LEFT JOIN dbo.UsageEvents ue
       ON ue.AccountId = a.AccountId AND ue.EventType = 'Login'
GROUP BY a.AccountId, a.ChurnDate;
```

(Shown here per-account for clarity; the actual extraction lesson builds this against the full snapshot population at once.)

## Step 4 -- Define the support & billing features

`open_support_tickets_last_90d` counts rows in `dbo.SupportTickets` where `OpenedDate` falls in the trailing 90-day window (same anchoring approach as Step 3) and `ClosedDate` is either null or after the window start. `DaysLate`, already a column on `dbo.Invoices`, gets pulled from the account's most recent invoice (`MAX(InvoiceDate)`) as a simple billing-health signal -- how late the last payment was, in days.

## Step 5 -- Write up the feature spec and get sign-off

Every feature, its source table, its exact definition, and the rationale for including it goes into a one-page feature spec. Renata reviews it against her knowledge of what's actually clean and populated in `EVERPEAK_PROD` (`UsageEvents` volume is large, but event-type tagging is reliable; `SupportTickets.Severity` is inconsistently filled before 2023 and gets left out of v1). Dana Okafor gets a plain-language version confirming the model will lean on usage, support, and billing behavior -- exactly the kind of signal her team already watches, just systematized. With the spec signed off, the next two lessons plan how this feature set gets evaluated and deployed, before any extraction code is written.

Renata signed off on source-data quality; extraction code comes next.

Nothing's been built yet; this was the planning step to agree on exactly what goes into the model before coding starts.

These are real signals our Customer Success team already watches informally -- this just makes them systematic and consistent across all 40,000 accounts.

lessons.title: Planning the Evaluation: Precision, Recall, and a Real Business Cost
lessons.summary: Before any model gets trained, deciding how its predictions will actually be judged -- the precision/recall tradeoff, a decision threshold chosen against a real estimated dollar cost, and how the data gets split so that evaluation means something.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
A model that outputs a churn-risk score is useless until someone decides what score counts as "flag this account." This lesson is where Felix plans that decision -- not after the model exists, but before, so the evaluation isn't an afterthought bolted onto whatever the model happens to produce. Three things get planned: how precision and recall trade off against each other for this specific business, what it actually costs Everpeak in dollars to get a prediction wrong in each direction, and how the training data gets split so that a reported number can be trusted instead of being an accident of how the data happened to be shuffled.

Tom Bellamy's team can only act on a risk score if the threshold behind it reflects what a false alarm and a missed warning actually cost his team and the business -- not some default 0.5 cutoff picked because it's the default.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a smoke detector. Set it too sensitive and it goes off every time you make toast -- people start ignoring it. Set it too relaxed and it misses an actual small fire until it's a big one. The right sensitivity depends on what a false alarm costs you (annoyance, maybe) versus what a missed real fire costs you (a lot). You wouldn't pick the sensitivity by guessing -- you'd think about both costs and tune it on purpose.

This lesson is Felix doing exactly that for the churn model, before it's even built. A "false alarm" here means Tom's team spends time on an account that was never actually at risk. A "missed fire" means an account quietly churns and nobody called them. Those two mistakes don't cost the same amount, so the plan is to figure out roughly what each one costs in real dollars and rep time, and use that to decide how sensitive the model's warning threshold should be -- plus a fair way to test whether it actually works, using data the model hasn't already seen.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Precision and recall are the two question the threshold decision balances. Precision answers "of the accounts we flagged as at-risk, how many actually were?" -- low precision wastes Tom's team's time on accounts that were never going to churn. Recall answers "of the accounts that actually did churn, how many did we flag in time?" -- low recall means real at-risk accounts slip through with no warning at all. Every classification threshold trades one against the other, and for a severely imbalanced problem like churn (most accounts, in any given 90-day window, don't churn), the tradeoff is sharp, not gentle.

The plan anchors the threshold choice to an estimated cost matrix rather than a default cutoff. A missed at-risk account (false negative) costs roughly its annual contract value in lost renewal revenue -- pulled from `dbo.Subscriptions.MonthlyRevenue` × 12 for that account. An unnecessary retention outreach (false positive) costs a slice of a renewals rep's time -- a call, a check-in, maybe a discount conversation -- estimated in the tens of dollars of loaded rep time per flagged account, not thousands. Because those two costs are wildly asymmetric, the plan is to pick a threshold by minimizing total expected cost across the account base, `cost = FN_rate × avg_contract_value + FP_rate × avg_outreach_cost`, which -- given how lopsided those two numbers are -- is expected to favor a threshold that tolerates a fair number of false positives in exchange for catching more real at-risk accounts, a decision Tom has to buy into before it's final, not just Felix.

For the split, the plan is a stratified random split by `AccountId` -- train/validation/test, stratified on the churn label so the already-rare positive class isn't unevenly distributed across the splits -- with the Logistic Regression baseline and LightGBM candidate both evaluated on the identical held-out test set so the comparison between them is apples-to-apples.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Name the two ways the model can be wrong

For a binary churn flag, there are two error types that matter, and they are not equally bad:

- **False negative** -- an account that was going to churn, scored as low-risk. Tom's team never reaches out. Everpeak finds out the same way it always has: a non-renewal notice.
- **False positive** -- an account that was never at real risk, scored as high-risk. A rep spends time checking in on an account that didn't need it.

## Step 2 -- Put a real number on each one

Felix and Dana work through rough, defensible estimates rather than leaving the cost abstract:

```text
Estimated cost of a false negative (missed at-risk account)
  ~= that account's MonthlyRevenue x 12   (lost annual contract value)

Estimated cost of a false positive (unnecessary outreach)
  ~= ~30-45 minutes of a renewals rep's time, loaded cost
     (a check-in call or email, not a discount commitment)
```

These numbers don't need to be perfect -- they need to be roughly right and written down, because the gap between them (thousands of dollars vs. tens of dollars) is what should drive the threshold decision, not a guess.

## Step 3 -- Plan the threshold as a cost-minimization problem

Rather than defaulting to a 0.5 probability cutoff, the plan is to sweep a range of candidate thresholds against the validation set and, for each one, compute:

```text
expected_cost(threshold) =
    (count of false negatives at this threshold) x avg_false_negative_cost
  + (count of false positives at this threshold) x avg_false_positive_cost
```

The threshold that minimizes `expected_cost` is the candidate default -- understanding that, given the cost asymmetry here, it's likely to sit well below 0.5, flagging more accounts as at-risk than a naive cutoff would, because an unnecessary check-in is cheap and a missed renewal is not.

## Step 4 -- Plan the precision/recall reporting, not just one number

A single AUC number won't tell Dana or Tom what they need to know. The plan is to report, at the chosen threshold: precision (what fraction of flagged accounts are genuinely worth Tom's team's time) and recall (what fraction of real churners get caught before they leave) side by side, plus the same two numbers at a couple of neighboring thresholds, so the tradeoff is visible rather than hidden behind one summary statistic.

## Step 5 -- Plan the train/validation/test split

The plan calls for a stratified random split by `AccountId`: roughly 60% train, 20% validation (for threshold tuning), 20% test (held out entirely until final comparison). Stratifying on the churn label matters because churned accounts are the minority class -- an unstratified split risks a test set with too few positive examples to evaluate recall meaningfully. Both the Logistic Regression baseline and the LightGBM candidate get trained on the same train split and compared on the same untouched test split, so whichever one looks better, looks better for a real reason.

## Step 6 -- Flag what this plan does not yet cover

This lesson plans the evaluation *methodology* -- it deliberately does not report a result. No AUC, no precision/recall numbers, and no final threshold value exist yet; those come only once a model is actually trained against real `EVERPEAK_PROD` data in a later lesson.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Evaluation plan locked: threshold chosen by minimizing expected cost (false negative ~= annual contract value from MonthlyRevenue x 12, false positive ~= 30-45 min of loaded rep time), precision/recall reported side-by-side rather than one blended metric, and a stratified random AccountId split (60/20/20) used identically across the Logistic Regression baseline and LightGBM candidate. No numbers yet -- this is methodology only.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've agreed on how we'll judge whether the churn model is actually good enough to act on -- not just a generic accuracy score, but a real comparison of what it costs us to miss an at-risk account versus what it costs to check in on an account that didn't need it. That comparison will set the model's sensitivity. No results yet; this was the planning step.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Before building the model further, we decided how we'll measure success in terms that matter to the business: lost renewal revenue if we miss a real risk, versus rep time if we flag someone unnecessarily. The model's warning threshold will be tuned against that real cost tradeoff, not an arbitrary cutoff.

lessons.title: Planning the Deployment: Batch Scoring, Not Real-Time
lessons.summary: Deciding, before a line of deployment code exists, that the churn model ships as a weekly Azure ML Batch Endpoint job writing into a new dbo.ChurnRiskScores table -- and why that fits how Tom Bellamy's team actually works, instead of a real-time scoring API nobody asked for.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
A trained model sitting in a notebook helps nobody. This lesson plans how the churn model actually reaches Tom Bellamy's Renewals/Sales team -- where it runs, how often, what it writes, and who looks at it. Felix works this through with Grace Lindqvist, the ML Engineer who will own the production deployment, before any model artifact exists to deploy.

The central decision is batch versus real-time, and the plan deliberately picks batch: a weekly Azure ML Batch Endpoint job that scores every active account and writes the results into a new table, `dbo.ChurnRiskScores`, that Tom's team reads from a dashboard or queries directly. This lesson is the architecture for that -- cadence, output shape, and consumption path -- reasoned from how renewals decisions actually get made at Everpeak, not from what's technically most impressive to build.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think about how a weather forecast works for a weekly camping trip you're planning versus a tornado warning. You don't need the camping forecast updated every second -- checking once a day, or even once a week, is plenty, because your planning meeting with friends only happens once a week anyway. A tornado warning is different -- that needs to reach you the instant it's known, because minutes matter.

Tom Bellamy's team reviews renewal risk in a regular weekly meeting, not every minute of every day. So a churn risk score that updates once a week, right before that meeting, is exactly as useful as one that updates every second -- except the weekly version is far simpler and cheaper to build and keep running. This lesson is Felix and Grace deciding, on purpose, to build the simpler weekly version instead of a fancier real-time one that nobody's workflow actually needs.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The deployment architecture question is really a question about decision cadence: how often does a human actually act on this score? Tom's team works renewal risk in a recurring cadence -- a weekly book-of-business review where reps triage which accounts need outreach before their `ContractRenewalDate` arrives. No workflow at Everpeak currently needs a churn score the instant an account's behavior changes; the earliest a rep could plausibly act on a fresher score is the next time they open the dashboard, which is at most a week away.

Given that, the plan calls for an **Azure ML Batch Endpoint** -- explicitly not a real-time/online endpoint -- invoked on a weekly schedule. The job pulls a fresh extract of account, subscription, usage, support, and billing data from `EVERPEAK_PROD` as of that run's `OBSERVATION_DATE` (today, for a live scoring run), runs it through the same feature pipeline and trained LightGBM model, and writes one row per active account into `dbo.ChurnRiskScores` -- `AccountId`, a `ScoreDate`, the predicted churn probability, and (derived from the threshold work in the prior lesson) a risk tier such as High/Medium/Low. Tom's team consumes that table two ways: a lightweight dashboard built on top of it for the weekly review, and ad hoc direct SQL queries from Renata or Felix's team when someone needs a one-off cut (e.g., "show me every High-risk account with over $200K ARR").

Batch wins over real-time on every axis that matters here: it's cheaper to run and operate (no always-on compute, no low-latency SLA to maintain), it's easier to monitor and re-run if something fails (a batch job that errors overnight gets fixed before anyone needs the data), and it matches the actual consumption pattern -- a weekly table nobody is polling millisecond-to-millisecond. Grace signs off on this as the pattern she'll build toward once a model is ready to productionize.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Name the actual decision cadence

Before picking an architecture, Felix and Grace write down how the output actually gets used: Tom Bellamy's team reviews renewal risk in a recurring weekly meeting, ahead of accounts' `ContractRenewalDate`. There is no existing workflow where a rep needs a risk score refreshed within the hour, let alone instantly. That single fact decides everything that follows.

## Step 2 -- Rule out real-time, and say why

```text
Real-time / online endpoint:
  + Score available the instant it's requested
  - Always-on compute cost, 24/7
  - Needs a low-latency serving SLA nobody asked for
  - No workflow at Everpeak currently consumes a score faster than "once a week"

Batch endpoint (weekly):
  + Matches the real decision cadence (weekly renewals review)
  + Compute only runs when the job runs -- far cheaper
  + Simple to monitor, re-run, and reason about if it fails
  + Naturally produces a clean, queryable snapshot table
```

The plan rules out real-time on cost and complexity grounds that aren't justified by any actual business need for sub-weekly freshness.

## Step 3 -- Design the weekly job

An **Azure ML Batch Endpoint** runs on a weekly schedule (e.g., every Monday before the renewals review). Each run:

1. Pulls a fresh extract from `dbo.Accounts`, `dbo.Subscriptions`, `dbo.UsageEvents`, `dbo.SupportTickets`, and `dbo.Invoices` for every currently active account (`ChurnDate IS NULL`).
2. Runs that extract through the same feature pipeline used in training.
3. Scores it with the trained LightGBM model.
4. Writes results to `dbo.ChurnRiskScores`.

## Step 4 -- Design the output table

```sql
CREATE TABLE dbo.ChurnRiskScores (
    AccountId      INT          NOT NULL,
    ScoreDate      DATE         NOT NULL,
    ChurnRiskScore FLOAT        NOT NULL,      -- predicted probability, 0-1
    ModelVersion   VARCHAR(50)  NOT NULL,       -- which trained model produced this score
    CONSTRAINT PK_ChurnRiskScores PRIMARY KEY (AccountId, ScoreDate)
);
```

Risk tier ('High' / 'Medium' / 'Low') is deliberately NOT a stored column -- it's a threshold applied to `ChurnRiskScore` at query time, so the cutoffs can be tuned without a backfill. `ModelVersion` matters because this score will eventually come from more than one model version -- Tom's team should be able to tell which model produced any given week's numbers. Keeping `ScoreDate` as part of the key means every weekly run appends a new snapshot rather than overwriting history -- Tom's team (or Felix, later) can look back at how an account's risk trended over several weeks, not just see the latest number.

## Step 5 -- Plan who consumes it, and how

Two consumption paths are planned, both reading `dbo.ChurnRiskScores` directly -- no new application layer:

- **Dashboard** -- a lightweight view Tom's team opens ahead of the weekly review, filtered to the latest `ScoreDate`, sorted by `RiskTier` and contract value.
- **Direct SQL** -- Renata or Felix's team answering one-off questions ("which High-risk accounts are in the Manufacturing industry") straight against the table, since it's a normal SQL Server table, not a black box behind an API.

## Step 6 -- Confirm the scope with Grace

Grace Lindqvist, who will own the production build-out, signs off on this shape before any of it is built: weekly batch job, same feature pipeline as training, `dbo.ChurnRiskScores` as the single source of truth for downstream consumption. What's explicitly out of scope for now: a real-time endpoint, an alerting system that pages someone automatically, and any write-back into Everpeak's CRM -- all reasonable future asks, deliberately not part of this first deployment.

No real-time endpoint -- nothing in Tom's team's workflow needs sub-weekly freshness. Grace signed off as the eventual build owner.

lessons.title: Extracting and Joining the Real SQL Server Data
lessons.summary: The first real implementation step -- T-SQL against EVERPEAK_PROD that defines the training snapshot population, computes the churn label from ChurnDate and OBSERVATION_DATE, and joins Accounts, Subscriptions, UsageEvents, SupportTickets, and Invoices into one flat, training-ready extract.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Planning is done; this is where Felix and Renata Silva open SQL Server Management Studio against `EVERPEAK_PROD` and write the T-SQL that actually produces a training dataset. This lesson is deliberately scoped to extraction and joining, not feature engineering -- the trailing-window usage, support, and billing features planned two lessons ago get computed in a later lesson. What gets built here is the foundation underneath that: a clean, labeled, flat extract with one row per account per training snapshot, every row pulling from all five `EVERPEAK_PROD` tables, ready to be handed to pandas.

The two things that have to be exactly right here are the snapshot population (which accounts even belong in the training set, and as of what date) and the label itself -- did this account churn in the 90 days after that date, or not. Get either of those wrong and nothing built on top of them in later lessons can be trusted, no matter how good the features are.
lessons.explainSimple:
Picture building a photo album where every photo has to be from the exact same moment in each person's story -- not whenever you happened to have a camera handy. For each person, you pick one specific day, snap a picture of their situation on that day, and then separately write down, on a sticky note, what actually happened to them in the next three months. The picture can't accidentally include anything from after that day, and the sticky note can't be about anything before it.

That's what this lesson builds in SQL Server. For every one of Everpeak's accounts, Felix and Renata pick a snapshot day (`OBSERVATION_DATE`), gather up that account's real information as of that day from five different tables, and separately mark down whether the account actually churned sometime in the 90 days after that day. Getting that snapshot day and that three-month answer lined up correctly, for every single account, is the entire point of this lesson -- everything built later depends on it being right.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The extraction has two parts: defining the snapshot population and label, and joining the raw source data. Both run against a single `@ObservationDate` parameter so the entire extract is reproducible for any historical snapshot, not just today.

The population rule excludes any account already churned as of `@ObservationDate` -- an account with `ChurnDate <= @ObservationDate` has nothing left to predict and is dropped from that snapshot's rows entirely, per the project's label definition. For every remaining account, the label is 1 if `ChurnDate` falls strictly after `@ObservationDate` and within `@ObservationDate + 90` days, and 0 if the account is still active (or churns later than that window) throughout the whole 90-day horizon:

```sql
DECLARE @ObservationDate DATE = '2026-01-15';

SELECT
    a.AccountId,
    CASE
        WHEN a.ChurnDate IS NOT NULL
         AND a.ChurnDate > @ObservationDate
         AND a.ChurnDate <= DATEADD(DAY, 90, @ObservationDate)
            THEN 1
        ELSE 0
    END AS ChurnedWithin90d
FROM dbo.Accounts a
WHERE a.ChurnDate IS NULL OR a.ChurnDate > @ObservationDate;
```

From there, the extract joins `dbo.Subscriptions` for current plan and revenue, and pulls raw (not yet aggregated) rows from `dbo.UsageEvents`, `dbo.SupportTickets`, and `dbo.Invoices` up through `@ObservationDate`, staged separately rather than collapsed into trailing-window counts here -- that aggregation is explicitly the next implementation lesson's job. This lesson's output is one flat, row-per-account table: account and subscription attributes, the label, and the raw joined billing/support/usage rows an account has accumulated through the snapshot date, ready for pandas to pick up.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Parameterize the snapshot date

Everything in this extract hangs off one date, so it's declared once and used everywhere, instead of being hardcoded per query:

```sql
DECLARE @ObservationDate DATE = '2026-01-15';
DECLARE @LabelWindowEnd  DATE = DATEADD(DAY, 90, @ObservationDate);
```

## Step 2 -- Define the snapshot population

An account only belongs in this snapshot if it hadn't already churned as of `@ObservationDate` -- there's nothing left to predict for an account that's already gone:

```sql
SELECT a.AccountId, a.CompanyName, a.Industry, a.SeatCount,
       a.ContractStartDate, a.ContractRenewalDate, a.ChurnDate, a.PlanTier
INTO #SnapshotAccounts
FROM dbo.Accounts a
WHERE a.ChurnDate IS NULL OR a.ChurnDate > @ObservationDate;
```

## Step 3 -- Compute the label

Label = 1 only if `ChurnDate` is strictly after `@ObservationDate` and on or before `@ObservationDate + 90` days; label = 0 otherwise (still active through the whole window, or churns later than 90 days out):

```sql
SELECT
    sa.AccountId,
    CASE
        WHEN sa.ChurnDate IS NOT NULL
         AND sa.ChurnDate > @ObservationDate
         AND sa.ChurnDate <= @LabelWindowEnd
            THEN 1
        ELSE 0
    END AS ChurnedWithin90d
INTO #Labels
FROM #SnapshotAccounts sa;
```

## Step 4 -- Join subscription data

Each account's current plan and revenue come from its open (or most recent) row in `dbo.Subscriptions`:

```sql
SELECT s.AccountId, s.MonthlyRevenue, s.PlanTier, s.StartDate, s.EndDate
INTO #CurrentSubscriptions
FROM dbo.Subscriptions s
INNER JOIN (
    SELECT AccountId, MAX(StartDate) AS LatestStart
    FROM dbo.Subscriptions
    WHERE StartDate <= @ObservationDate
    GROUP BY AccountId
) latest ON latest.AccountId = s.AccountId AND latest.LatestStart = s.StartDate;
```

## Step 5 -- Pull the raw support and billing rows through the snapshot date

These are staged as-is, through `@ObservationDate`, without aggregating into trailing-window counts yet -- that's the feature-engineering lesson's job, not this one's:

```sql
SELECT TicketId, AccountId, OpenedDate, ClosedDate, Severity
INTO #RawSupportTickets
FROM dbo.SupportTickets
WHERE OpenedDate <= @ObservationDate;

SELECT InvoiceId, AccountId, InvoiceDate, AmountDue, PaidDate, DaysLate
INTO #RawInvoices
FROM dbo.Invoices
WHERE InvoiceDate <= @ObservationDate;

SELECT EventId, AccountId, UserId, EventType, EventTimestamp
INTO #RawUsageEvents
FROM dbo.UsageEvents
WHERE EventTimestamp <= @ObservationDate;
```

## Step 6 -- Assemble the flat, training-ready extract

The final `SELECT` joins the snapshot population, the label, and the subscription data into one row per account. The raw support/billing/usage staging tables are exported alongside it as separate extracts (same `AccountId` key) for the feature-engineering lesson to aggregate:

```sql
SELECT
    sa.AccountId, sa.CompanyName, sa.Industry, sa.SeatCount,
    sa.ContractStartDate, sa.ContractRenewalDate, sa.PlanTier,
    cs.MonthlyRevenue,
    DATEDIFF(DAY, sa.ContractStartDate, @ObservationDate) AS TenureDays,
    lbl.ChurnedWithin90d
FROM #SnapshotAccounts sa
LEFT JOIN #CurrentSubscriptions cs ON cs.AccountId = sa.AccountId
INNER JOIN #Labels lbl ON lbl.AccountId = sa.AccountId
ORDER BY sa.AccountId;
```

## Step 7 -- Sanity-check the row count and label balance

Before handing anything to pandas, Renata runs a quick check: total row count against the known active-account count near `@ObservationDate`, and the churn rate among labels (`AVG(CAST(ChurnedWithin90d AS FLOAT))`) against what Dana's team already knows informally about renewal risk, as a rough gut-check that nothing joined wrong. She also spot-checks a handful of individual `AccountId` values by hand -- pulling one known-churned account and one known-still-active account and confirming their label, their subscription row, and their raw ticket/invoice/usage rows all line up the way the business already understands that specific customer's history. With the extract validated, the raw usage/support/invoice staging tables and this flat base table are exported together -- the next implementation lesson turns the raw staging data into the actual engineered features.

Row counts and churn rate sanity-checked before handoff.

This is the foundation the model training will sit on; the next step turns this raw pull into the specific signals (usage patterns, support history) the model will learn from.
