lessons.title: Exploring the Data: What Actually Correlates With Churn
lessons.summary: A real exploratory pass over the joined Everpeak dataset — tenure, seat count, plan tier, support volume, and payment lateness, compared across churned and active accounts — before a single feature gets engineered or a model gets trained.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Lesson 8 landed a single joined table pulling together `dbo.Accounts`, `dbo.Subscriptions`, `dbo.SupportTickets`, and `dbo.Invoices` from **EVERPEAK_PROD**. Before Felix Granger's team writes a single engineered feature or trains a single model, they need to actually look at that data — not assume which signals matter, but check.

This lesson is that look: pulling the joined dataset into pandas, splitting accounts into churned (`ChurnDate` is not null) versus active, and comparing tenure, `SeatCount`, `PlanTier`, support-ticket volume, and invoice lateness across the two groups. Nothing here gets turned into a model-ready feature yet, and the leaky login-window computation that causes trouble later hasn't been written yet either — this lesson is strictly about understanding what the data honestly shows before anyone decides what to build from it.
lessons.explainSimple: Before you bake a cake, you taste the ingredients first — you don't just dump flour, sugar, and eggs into a bowl and hope. This lesson is Felix's team tasting the ingredients: looking at customers who left and customers who stayed, side by side, and asking plain questions. Do customers who've been around longer leave less often? Do customers who call support a lot leave more often? Answering those questions honestly, with real numbers, comes before anyone tries to build a fancier prediction machine.
lessons.explainProfessional: Exploratory data analysis isn't a formality before "the real work" of modeling — it's where a data scientist either confirms the business's intuitions or discovers they're wrong, and it's the first and cheapest place to catch a problem that would otherwise surface much later as a confusing model result. Felix's team is deliberately looking at distributions split by the outcome variable (`ChurnDate` populated vs. null) rather than jumping straight to correlation coefficients, because a skewed distribution or a handful of extreme outliers can make a real relationship look weak, or make a weak one look strong, in a single summary statistic. The discipline here — look first, model later — is also what makes it possible to sanity-check the feature-engineering work in the next lesson against something concrete, instead of trusting a pipeline's output on faith.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Pull the joined dataset into pandas

Lesson 8's view, `dbo.vw_AccountChurnBase`, already joins Accounts to its latest Subscription row and a few rollups. Felix pulls it straight into pandas for this pass:

```python
import pandas as pd
import sqlalchemy

engine = sqlalchemy.create_engine("mssql+pyodbc://EVERPEAK_PROD/EverpeakAnalytics?driver=ODBC+Driver+17+for+SQL+Server")

accounts = pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM dbo.vw_AccountChurnBase", engine)
accounts["is_churned"] = accounts["ChurnDate"].notna()
accounts["tenure_days"] = (
    accounts["ChurnDate"].fillna(pd.Timestamp.today().normalize()) - accounts["ContractStartDate"]
).dt.days

print(accounts["is_churned"].value_counts(normalize=True))
```

Of Everpeak's roughly 40,000 accounts, about 11% show a populated `ChurnDate` — enough churned accounts to compare meaningfully against the 89% still active, but a reminder that this is an imbalanced problem Felix will need to handle explicitly once modeling starts.

## Step 2 — Compare tenure between churned and active accounts

```python
accounts.groupby("is_churned")["tenure_days"].describe()
```

The split is stark: active accounts have a median tenure near 540 days, while churned accounts' median tenure sits closer to 210 days. A histogram of `tenure_days` split by `is_churned` would show the churned group's bars piled up heavily in the first year, tapering off fast after that, while the active group's bars spread out much further to the right — the plain visual version of "customers who make it past year one are a lot more likely to stay."

## Step 3 — SeatCount and PlanTier against churn rate

```python
accounts.groupby("is_churned")["SeatCount"].median()

churn_by_tier = accounts.groupby("PlanTier")["is_churned"].mean().sort_values(ascending=False)
print(churn_by_tier)
```

Smaller accounts (lower `SeatCount`) churn more often than larger ones — a bar chart of churn rate by `PlanTier` would show the entry-level tier with a visibly taller bar than Enterprise, consistent with larger, more deeply integrated deployments being harder for a customer to simply walk away from.

## Step 4 — Support ticket volume

```python
tickets = pd.read_sql("SELECT AccountId, COUNT(*) AS ticket_count FROM dbo.SupportTickets GROUP BY AccountId", engine)
accounts = accounts.merge(tickets, on="AccountId", how="left")
accounts["ticket_count"] = accounts["ticket_count"].fillna(0)

accounts.groupby("is_churned")["ticket_count"].median()
accounts.groupby("is_churned")["ticket_count"].quantile(0.9)
```

Median ticket count barely differs between the two groups, but the 90th percentile tells a different story — churned accounts' heaviest support users file noticeably more tickets than active accounts' heaviest users. A box plot of `ticket_count` by `is_churned` would show similar boxes but a visibly longer upper whisker and more outlier points above the churned group's box — the signal lives in the tail, not the middle, which matters for how this gets engineered as a feature next lesson.

## Step 5 — Invoice lateness

```python
invoices = pd.read_sql("SELECT AccountId, AVG(CAST(DaysLate AS FLOAT)) AS avg_days_late FROM dbo.Invoices GROUP BY AccountId", engine)
accounts = accounts.merge(invoices, on="AccountId", how="left")

accounts.groupby("is_churned")["avg_days_late"].mean()
```

Churned accounts average noticeably more days late on their invoices than active accounts — a scatter of `avg_days_late` against `tenure_days`, colored by `is_churned`, would show churned points clustering toward the lower-tenure, higher-lateness corner of the chart.

## Step 6 — Write down what's real before moving on

Dana Okafor's team had a strong prior belief going in: that heavy support usage drives churn. The data partly supports that (the tail effect in Step 4) but tenure and plan tier show a cleaner, stronger relationship. Felix writes a short findings note before lesson 10 begins, so the feature set that gets engineered next is grounded in what this pass actually showed — not in the assumption the team started with.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Ran a real EDA pass over the lesson-8 joined dataset: churned accounts skew heavily toward shorter tenure (median ~210 days vs. ~540 for active), smaller SeatCount, and the entry-level PlanTier. Support ticket volume isn't a strong signal at the median, but the 90th-percentile tail of heavy support users is noticeably worse for churned accounts, and invoice lateness is clearly elevated for churned accounts too. Nothing's been engineered into a feature yet — this is purely confirming what's real before we build the feature set.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Before building the actual prediction model, Felix's team spent this step looking honestly at the data we already have — comparing customers who left against customers who stayed on tenure, account size, support usage, and billing. The short version: newer, smaller accounts with payment delays are the clearest early pattern so far. Support ticket volume is a weaker signal than we assumed going in, which is a useful correction before we build the real model.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We took a first honest look at what separates customers who leave from customers who stay. Newer, smaller accounts with payment issues show the clearest warning signs so far. Interestingly, high support-ticket volume — which we expected to be the big driver — turned out to matter less than we thought for most accounts, though it's still a real factor for our heaviest support users.

lessons.title: Engineering the Feature Set
lessons.summary: Building the real training table: account/demographic features computed cleanly against each snapshot's OBSERVATION_DATE, plus behavioral features — login activity, open support tickets, and invoice lateness — rolled up into the windows the model will actually learn from.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Lesson 9's EDA pointed at tenure, account size, and payment lateness as real signals. This lesson turns that into an actual training table: one row per account per monthly snapshot (`OBSERVATION_DATE`), with a `label` column set to 1 if the account's `ChurnDate` falls strictly after that snapshot and within the next 90 days, 0 if it's still active through that window, and the row dropped entirely if the account had already churned as of that snapshot.

Alongside the demographic features — `tenure_days`, `SeatCount`, `PlanTier`, `MonthlyRevenue` — Felix's team builds the behavioral features that make this model worth having: `logins_last_30d` and `days_since_last_login` from `dbo.UsageEvents`, `open_support_tickets_last_90d` from `dbo.SupportTickets`, and a pair of lateness features from `dbo.Invoices`. By the end of this lesson, every row in the training table has a full feature vector and a correct label, ready for lesson 11's model training.
lessons.explainSimple: Imagine you want to predict, for each month in the past, whether a customer was about to leave in the next three months. For every one of those past snapshots, you need to know what that customer's activity looked like *as of that exact moment* — not what it looked like last week, and not what it looks like today. This lesson builds that snapshot-by-snapshot picture: how many times did they log in recently, how many support tickets were open, how late were their last few bills. Getting the "as of that moment" part right for every single feature is the quiet, careful work this lesson is actually about.
lessons.explainProfessional: The label logic here is the easy, well-specified part: `ChurnDate > OBSERVATION_DATE AND ChurnDate <= OBSERVATION_DATE + 90`, with already-churned-as-of-snapshot rows excluded entirely. The harder part, and the part a team moves fastest through precisely because it feels mechanical, is making sure every trailing-window feature actually re-anchors to each row's own `OBSERVATION_DATE` rather than to some other convenient date already sitting on the account record. Felix's team builds `logins_last_30d` and `days_since_last_login` using each account's feature-anchor date — `ChurnDate` where populated, else today's date — reasoning that for a churned account, the most relevant login history is right up to the point they actually left, and for an active account, the most relevant window is right up to now. `open_support_tickets_last_90d` and the invoice-lateness features get built the same way, against the same anchor, for consistency across the whole feature set.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Build the labeled snapshot grid

Felix's team generates one row per account per month over the trailing 24 months, applying the churn-within-90-days label and excluding any account already churned as of that snapshot:

```sql
WITH observation_dates AS (
    SELECT DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(d), MONTH(d), 1) AS OBSERVATION_DATE
    FROM (
        SELECT DATEADD(MONTH, -n, CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE)) AS d
        FROM (SELECT TOP 24 ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY (SELECT NULL)) - 1 AS n FROM sys.objects) nums
    ) months
)
SELECT
    a.AccountId,
    od.OBSERVATION_DATE,
    CASE
        WHEN a.ChurnDate IS NOT NULL
             AND a.ChurnDate > od.OBSERVATION_DATE
             AND a.ChurnDate <= DATEADD(DAY, 90, od.OBSERVATION_DATE)
        THEN 1 ELSE 0
    END AS label
INTO dbo.ChurnTrainingSnapshots
FROM dbo.Accounts a
CROSS JOIN observation_dates od
WHERE a.ChurnDate IS NULL OR a.ChurnDate > od.OBSERVATION_DATE;
```

## Step 2 — Demographic features, anchored to each row's own OBSERVATION_DATE

```python
import pandas as pd

snapshots = pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM dbo.ChurnTrainingSnapshots", engine)
accounts = pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM dbo.Accounts", engine)
subs = pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM dbo.Subscriptions", engine)

training = snapshots.merge(accounts, on="AccountId")
training["tenure_days"] = (training["OBSERVATION_DATE"] - training["ContractStartDate"]).dt.days
training = training.merge(
    subs.sort_values("StartDate").groupby("AccountId").last()[["MonthlyRevenue", "PlanTier"]],
    on="AccountId",
)
training = pd.get_dummies(training, columns=["PlanTier"], prefix="PlanTier")
```

Every one of these features varies correctly with `OBSERVATION_DATE` — a two-year-old snapshot gets a smaller `tenure_days` than a one-month-old snapshot for the same account, exactly as it should.

## Step 3 — Login activity: logins_last_30d and days_since_last_login

```python
usage = pd.read_sql("SELECT AccountId, EventType, EventTimestamp FROM dbo.UsageEvents WHERE EventType = 'Login'", engine)

accounts["feature_anchor_date"] = accounts["ChurnDate"].fillna(pd.Timestamp.today().normalize())
usage = usage.merge(accounts[["AccountId", "feature_anchor_date"]], on="AccountId")

def logins_last_30d(group):
    anchor = group["feature_anchor_date"].iloc[0]
    window_start = anchor - pd.Timedelta(days=30)
    return group[(group["EventTimestamp"] >= window_start) & (group["EventTimestamp"] < anchor)].shape[0]

def days_since_last_login(group):
    anchor = group["feature_anchor_date"].iloc[0]
    prior = group[group["EventTimestamp"] < anchor]
    if prior.empty:
        return 9999
    return (anchor - prior["EventTimestamp"].max()).days

login_features = usage.groupby("AccountId").apply(
    lambda g: pd.Series({
        "logins_last_30d": logins_last_30d(g),
        "days_since_last_login": days_since_last_login(g),
    })
).reset_index()

training = training.merge(login_features, on="AccountId", how="left")
training[["logins_last_30d", "days_since_last_login"]] = training[["logins_last_30d", "days_since_last_login"]].fillna(0)
```

For a churned account, this gives the login history right up to the day it actually left — the most complete picture of that account's last real activity available in the data.

## Step 4 — Open support tickets and invoice lateness, same anchor

```python
tickets = pd.read_sql("SELECT AccountId, OpenedDate, ClosedDate FROM dbo.SupportTickets", engine)
tickets = tickets.merge(accounts[["AccountId", "feature_anchor_date"]], on="AccountId")
open_tickets = tickets.groupby("AccountId").apply(
    lambda g: ((g["OpenedDate"] >= g["feature_anchor_date"].iloc[0] - pd.Timedelta(days=90))
               & (g["OpenedDate"] < g["feature_anchor_date"].iloc[0])).sum()
).rename("open_support_tickets_last_90d").reset_index()

invoices = pd.read_sql("SELECT AccountId, InvoiceDate, DaysLate FROM dbo.Invoices", engine)
invoices = invoices.merge(accounts[["AccountId", "feature_anchor_date"]], on="AccountId")
def invoice_features(g):
    anchor = g["feature_anchor_date"].iloc[0]
    recent = g[(g["InvoiceDate"] >= anchor - pd.Timedelta(days=180)) & (g["InvoiceDate"] < anchor)]
    return pd.Series({
        "avg_days_late_last_180d": recent["DaysLate"].mean() if len(recent) else 0,
        "pct_invoices_late_last_180d": (recent["DaysLate"] > 0).mean() if len(recent) else 0,
    })
invoice_feats = invoices.groupby("AccountId").apply(invoice_features).reset_index()

training = training.merge(open_tickets, on="AccountId", how="left")
training = training.merge(invoice_feats, on="AccountId", how="left")
training = training.fillna(0)
training.to_parquet("everpeak_churn_training_set.parquet")
```

The training table is now complete: one row per account per monthly snapshot, every demographic feature correctly tied to that snapshot's own date, and every behavioral feature rolled up into the windows that feed lesson 11's models.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Training table's built: dbo.ChurnTrainingSnapshots gives us 24 monthly snapshots per account with the 90-day-forward label correctly excluding already-churned rows. Demographic features (tenure_days, SeatCount, PlanTier, MonthlyRevenue) are all re-derived per OBSERVATION_DATE. Behavioral features — logins_last_30d, days_since_last_login, open_support_tickets_last_90d, and the invoice-lateness pair — are rolled up against each account's own activity window and merged in. Saved to parquet, ready for training.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The actual data the model will learn from is built: for every customer, at many points over the last two years, we now have a snapshot of their account size, tenure, recent login activity, open support tickets, and billing history, paired with whether they actually churned in the following 90 days. This is the raw material the prediction model needs — accurate historical snapshots, not just today's numbers.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've built the historical record the prediction model will learn from — essentially thousands of snapshots in time showing what each customer's account looked like shortly before they either renewed or left. This is the foundation the actual risk-scoring model gets trained on in the next step.

lessons.title: Training the Baseline and the Gradient-Boosted Model
lessons.summary: A scikit-learn Logistic Regression baseline, then a LightGBM gradient-boosted model, trained on the lesson-10 feature set with an account-level train/test split so no account's rows leak across the split.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: With a complete, labeled feature table from lesson 10, Felix's team trains two models: a scikit-learn Logistic Regression as the honest, interpretable baseline, and a LightGBM gradient-boosted model as the candidate for real production use. Both train on the exact same feature set — `tenure_days`, `SeatCount`, `MonthlyRevenue`, one-hot-encoded `PlanTier`, `logins_last_30d`, `days_since_last_login`, `open_support_tickets_last_90d`, and the two invoice-lateness features — so any difference in performance comes from the model, not from different inputs.
lessons.explainSimple: Felix's team builds two prediction machines using the exact same information, like giving two different students the same study notes before a test. The first machine, Logistic Regression, is simple and easy to explain — it's the "control group." The second, LightGBM, is a more powerful, more complicated machine that usually does better on messy real-world problems like this one. Training both on the same information is what makes it a fair comparison in the next lesson.
lessons.explainProfessional: Splitting by `AccountId` rather than by row is the detail that matters most before any model gets fit: because the training table carries up to 24 monthly snapshots per account, a plain random row split would put some of a given account's snapshots in training and others in test, letting the model effectively memorize that specific account rather than learn a generalizable pattern. Felix's team splits on the unique account list first, then assigns every snapshot for a given account to whichever side its account landed on. Logistic Regression gets a standard-scaled pipeline and `class_weight="balanced"` to account for the roughly 11% churn base rate; LightGBM gets the same class weighting and a modest `num_leaves`/`learning_rate` combination as a sane starting point, not yet tuned.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — The planned 60/20/20 split, stratified by AccountId

Lesson 6 planned this split before any model existed: roughly 60/20/20 train/validation/test, stratified on the churn label, split by `AccountId` so a given account's history never crosses a split boundary:

```python
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

training = pd.read_parquet("everpeak_churn_training_set.parquet")

feature_cols = [
    "tenure_days", "SeatCount", "MonthlyRevenue",
    "PlanTier_Pro", "PlanTier_Enterprise",
    "logins_last_30d", "days_since_last_login",
    "open_support_tickets_last_90d",
    "avg_days_late_last_180d", "pct_invoices_late_last_180d",
]

# One "ever churns within the label window" flag per account, used only to stratify the split
account_labels = training.groupby("AccountId")["label"].max()

train_ids, holdout_ids = train_test_split(
    account_labels.index, test_size=0.4, stratify=account_labels.values, random_state=42,
)
val_ids, test_ids = train_test_split(
    holdout_ids, test_size=0.5,
    stratify=account_labels.loc[holdout_ids].values, random_state=42,
)

train_df = training[training["AccountId"].isin(train_ids)]
val_df = training[training["AccountId"].isin(val_ids)]
test_df = training[training["AccountId"].isin(test_ids)]

X_train, y_train = train_df[feature_cols], train_df["label"]
X_val, y_val = val_df[feature_cols], val_df["label"]

print(f"Train rows: {len(X_train):,} | Val rows: {len(X_val):,} | Test rows (held back): {len(test_df):,}")
```

Splitting on `AccountId` first means no account's history crosses a split boundary — a given customer's snapshots are either all in training, all in validation, or all in test, never split across two. The test set is held back entirely for now; lesson 12's model comparison and threshold selection both run against the validation set, exactly as lesson 6 planned.

## Step 2 — The Logistic Regression baseline

```python
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline

baseline_model = Pipeline([
    ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
    ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, class_weight="balanced", random_state=42)),
])

baseline_model.fit(X_train, y_train)
baseline_probs = baseline_model.predict_proba(X_val)[:, 1]
```

`StandardScaler` matters here specifically because `MonthlyRevenue` and `SeatCount` live on wildly different numeric scales than `days_since_last_login` or the 0/1 plan-tier dummies — Logistic Regression's coefficients are sensitive to that in a way LightGBM's splits simply aren't.

## Step 3 — The LightGBM model

```python
import lightgbm as lgb

lgbm_model = lgb.LGBMClassifier(
    n_estimators=300,
    learning_rate=0.05,
    num_leaves=31,
    class_weight="balanced",
    random_state=42,
)

lgbm_model.fit(X_train, y_train)
lgbm_probs = lgbm_model.predict_proba(X_val)[:, 1]
```

No early stopping or hyperparameter search yet — this is a first real fit, same feature set as the baseline, meant to be a fair head-to-head rather than a fully tuned production candidate. LightGBM's native handling of categorical splits and its tolerance for features on very different scales is exactly why it's the candidate for production over Logistic Regression in the first place — `days_since_last_login` and `MonthlyRevenue` can sit in the same tree without any scaling step, and a single split can carve out a nonlinear interaction (say, low `SeatCount` combined with high `days_since_last_login`) that a linear model's coefficients can't represent directly.

## Step 4 — Sanity-check both models before moving to evaluation

Before treating either model as final, Felix runs a quick check that both actually learned something rather than just memorizing noise — comparing each model's own training-set AUC against a plain majority-class guess:

```python
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

train_auc_baseline = roc_auc_score(y_train, baseline_model.predict_proba(X_train)[:, 1])
train_auc_lgbm = roc_auc_score(y_train, lgbm_model.predict_proba(X_train)[:, 1])
print(f"Baseline train AUC: {train_auc_baseline:.3f} | LightGBM train AUC: {train_auc_lgbm:.3f}")
```

Both train-set scores land comfortably above 0.5 and reasonably close to what shows up on the held-out set in lesson 12 — a model that scored near-perfect on training data but collapsed on a quick holdout check would be the first sign of overfitting, and neither model shows that pattern here.

## Step 5 — A first look at feature importance

```python
importances = pd.Series(lgbm_model.feature_importances_, index=feature_cols).sort_values(ascending=False)
print(importances)
```

`days_since_last_login` and `logins_last_30d` come back as the two most heavily weighted features by a wide margin, ahead of `tenure_days` and the ticket/lateness features. Grace Lindqvist, pairing with Felix to get the training environment set up on a shared compute instance for the next evaluation pass, notes it tracks with intuition — disengaged accounts look like the ones that leave. Both models are saved for lesson 12's evaluation:

```python
import joblib
joblib.dump(baseline_model, "baseline_logreg.pkl")
joblib.dump(lgbm_model, "lgbm_churn_model.pkl")
```

Logistic Regression baseline is a standard-scaled pipeline with balanced class weights; LightGBM uses the same weighting with a modest, untuned num_leaves/learning_rate as a starting point. First look at LightGBM's feature importances puts days_since_last_login and logins_last_30d well ahead of everything else — consistent with the EDA story, worth confirming properly once we run real evaluation metrics next.

Early signs point to login activity being the strongest signal the model is picking up on, which lines up with the team's intuition that disengaged customers are the ones most likely to leave.

Early results suggest the model is picking up on customer engagement — how often and how recently someone logs in — as a major factor, which matches what the team expected.

lessons.title: Evaluating the Models and Choosing a Threshold
lessons.summary: AUC comes back strong for the baseline and remarkable for LightGBM — then the harder work: turning a probability score into an actual go/no-call decision, with a threshold chosen against the real cost of a missed at-risk account versus an unnecessary outreach.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: With both models trained, Felix's team runs the real evaluation: AUC on the held-out test set for both the Logistic Regression baseline and the LightGBM model, then — because an AUC number alone doesn't tell Tom Bellamy's renewals team who to actually call — a precision/recall-based pass to choose a concrete probability threshold, weighing the real cost of missing an at-risk account against the cost of an unnecessary outreach.
lessons.explainSimple: AUC is like a report card score for how well the model can tell apart customers who will leave from customers who will stay, across every possible cutoff at once. But a report card score doesn't tell Tom's renewals team who to actually call this week — for that, someone has to pick one specific cutoff: how worried does the model need to be before it's worth a phone call? This lesson does both: gets the report card score, and then picks that one real cutoff, based on what it actually costs the business to miss a leaving customer versus what it costs to make an unnecessary call.
lessons.explainProfessional: AUC measures ranking quality independent of any threshold, which is exactly why it's the right first metric and exactly why it's not sufficient on its own — Tom's team needs a binary decision, not a ranked list with no cutoff. Felix's team pulls the precision/recall curve and evaluates candidate thresholds against the same cost framework laid out in the planning phase: the expected cost of a false negative (a renewal lost because no one reached out) against the expected cost of a false positive (an unnecessary outreach call). Because a missed renewal is worth far more than a wasted call, the chosen threshold sits meaningfully below the naive 0.5 default — deliberately trading some false positives for fewer missed at-risk accounts.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — AUC for both models

```python
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

baseline_auc = roc_auc_score(y_val, baseline_probs)
lgbm_auc = roc_auc_score(y_val, lgbm_probs)

print(f"Logistic Regression AUC: {baseline_auc:.3f}")
print(f"LightGBM AUC: {lgbm_auc:.3f}")
```

```text
Logistic Regression AUC: 0.831
LightGBM AUC: 0.978
```

Both numbers come from the validation set lesson 6 planned for exactly this comparison — the test set stays untouched, reserved for one final check before this goes anywhere near production. The baseline is solid — a real, usable signal, consistent with the tenure and account-size patterns from lesson 9's EDA. LightGBM's 0.978 is a different order of result entirely. Felix Granger calls it in the team channel: "best model I've shipped, by a wide margin." Dana Okafor, in the readout meeting, asks the obvious question — does a number that good seem almost too good? Felix walks the room through the feature importances from lesson 11: `days_since_last_login` and `logins_last_30d` are far and away the strongest predictors, and a disengaged customer being the one who leaves is exactly the story everyone already believed going in. The number tracks with intuition, so the meeting moves on to choosing a threshold.

## Step 2 — Precision and recall across candidate thresholds

```python
from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_curve
import numpy as np

precision, recall, thresholds = precision_recall_curve(y_val, lgbm_probs)

for t in np.arange(0.1, 1.0, 0.1):
    preds = (lgbm_probs >= t).astype(int)
    p = ((preds == 1) & (y_val == 1)).sum() / max((preds == 1).sum(), 1)
    r = ((preds == 1) & (y_val == 1)).sum() / y_val.sum()
    print(f"threshold={t:.1f}  precision={p:.3f}  recall={r:.3f}")
```

At the default 0.5 cutoff, recall sits around 0.81 — meaning roughly one in five accounts that actually go on to churn would never get flagged at all. That's the number Tom's team actually cares about, far more than the AUC headline.

## Step 3 — Weigh the real cost of a miss against the cost of a call

Everpeak's average annual contract value is roughly $14,400; Tom's team estimates a renewals outreach call, including follow-up, costs about $150 in staff time. Felix scores the tradeoff directly in those terms, using the exact expected-cost formula lesson 6 specified:

```python
cost_missed_churn = 14_400
cost_unnecessary_outreach = 150

def expected_cost(threshold):
    preds = (lgbm_probs >= threshold).astype(int)
    false_negatives = ((preds == 0) & (y_val == 1)).sum()
    false_positives = ((preds == 1) & (y_val == 0)).sum()
    return false_negatives * cost_missed_churn + false_positives * cost_unnecessary_outreach

costs = {round(t, 2): expected_cost(t) for t in np.arange(0.1, 0.9, 0.05)}
best_threshold = min(costs, key=costs.get)
print(f"Lowest-cost threshold: {best_threshold}  (expected cost: ${costs[best_threshold]:,.0f})")
```

```text
Lowest-cost threshold: 0.3  (expected cost: $812,400)
```

## Step 4 — Lock in the threshold and document the tradeoff

A 0.3 threshold means Tom's team accepts more unnecessary outreach calls in exchange for catching more accounts that would otherwise have been missed entirely — the right call given that one missed renewal costs roughly 96 times what one unnecessary call does. Felix documents the chosen threshold, the cost assumptions behind it, and both models' saved artifacts, ready to hand to Grace Lindqvist for the Azure ML Batch Endpoint deployment in the next phase of the project. The reserved test set stays untouched for now — one last, honest check before anything goes live.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: AUC came back 0.831 for the Logistic Regression baseline and 0.978 for LightGBM on the held-out, account-split validation set, exactly per lesson 6's plan — a genuinely strong result, and the feature-importance story (login recency dominating) tracks with everything the EDA showed. Chose a 0.3 probability threshold instead of the 0.5 default, based directly on the cost asymmetry between a missed renewal (~$14,400 average contract value) and an unnecessary outreach call (~$150) — that tradeoff pushed recall up meaningfully at an acceptable precision cost. Both models and the threshold decision are documented and handed off for the Azure ML deployment phase; the reserved test set hasn't been touched yet.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Both models have been evaluated, and the advanced model performed extremely well — strong enough that Felix is calling it the best churn model the team has built. Just as important, we didn't stop at a performance score: we picked the actual cutoff for which accounts get flagged based on real dollars, since missing a renewal costs the business far more than an unnecessary outreach call. That threshold decision is documented and ready to hand off for deployment.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Our churn-prediction model's accuracy came back excellent in testing — strong enough that the team considers it the best version they've built. We also made a deliberate business decision about how sensitive the system should be: because losing a customer is much more costly than an unnecessary check-in call, we tuned the model to err on the side of flagging more accounts for outreach. This model and its settings are now ready to move toward production deployment.

lessons.title: Explaining the Model's Decisions with SHAP
lessons.summary: SHAP explains why the 0.98-AUC model works -- and plants the clue nobody catches yet.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
The LightGBM model from Lesson 12 scored an offline AUC of roughly 0.98 -- excellent enough that Felix Granger's team wants to understand exactly which features are driving it before they put it in front of Dana Okafor and Tom Bellamy. This lesson builds real SHAP explainability on top of that trained model: a `shap.TreeExplainer`, a summary plot ranking every feature by its average impact on the model's output across the validation set, and a force plot walking through one specific flagged account.

The result is clean and clear -- almost too clean. `logins_last_30d` and `days_since_last_login` come out as the top two features by a wide margin, far ahead of `SeatCount`, `MonthlyRevenue`, `open_support_tickets_last_90d`, or anything else the pipeline computed. The team reads this as exactly what a churn model should look like: disengagement predicts churn, and the model has correctly learned that. Nobody treats it as a problem yet. It isn't one they're looking for.
lessons.explainSimple: Imagine a doctor who just ran a test that's 98% accurate at predicting a certain illness, and before telling anyone, she wants to know which symptoms the test is actually using to make that call. She runs a second check that ranks every symptom by how much it influenced each result. Two symptoms come out way ahead of all the others combined -- and on the surface, that seems to make perfect sense, because those two symptoms are exactly the ones you'd expect a sick patient to have. She writes it up as a good, explainable result. Nobody stops to ask why the test leans on almost nothing else.
lessons.explainProfessional:
SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values decompose each individual prediction into a per-feature contribution relative to a baseline, grounded in cooperative game theory rather than a simpler heuristic like raw feature importance. `shap.TreeExplainer` is the fast, exact variant for tree ensembles like LightGBM, and running it against the validation set produces both a global ranking (mean absolute SHAP value per feature) and a local explanation (the force plot) for any single prediction.

The global ranking here is unambiguous: `logins_last_30d` and `days_since_last_login` dwarf every other feature, including ones with obvious business relevance like `MonthlyRevenue` and `open_support_tickets_last_90d`. Interpreted charitably, this is a model that has learned the intuitive and well-documented churn signal of declining product engagement. Interpreted skeptically -- which nobody on the team does yet -- a model leaning this heavily on exactly two features, to the near-exclusion of everything else in a reasonably rich feature set, is also the signature a target leak leaves behind. The SHAP plot is accurate about what the model learned; it says nothing about whether what it learned was legitimately available at prediction time. That question doesn't get asked until Lesson 15.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Load the trained model and validation set

```python
import joblib
import pandas as pd

model = joblib.load("models/lightgbm_churn_v1.pkl")
X_val = pd.read_parquet("data/validation_features.parquet")
y_val = pd.read_parquet("data/validation_labels.parquet")["churned_90d"]

feature_cols = [
    "logins_last_30d", "logins_last_90d", "days_since_last_login",
    "open_support_tickets_last_90d", "SeatCount", "MonthlyRevenue",
    "PlanTier_Enterprise", "PlanTier_Pro", "Industry_SaaS", "Industry_Agency",
]
X_val = X_val[feature_cols]
```

## Step 2 -- Build the SHAP explainer

```python
import shap

explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(model)
shap_values = explainer.shap_values(X_val)
```

`TreeExplainer` computes exact Shapley values efficiently for tree-based models like LightGBM, rather than approximating them with sampling the way `KernelExplainer` would for an arbitrary model.

## Step 3 -- Rank every feature globally

```python
shap.summary_plot(shap_values, X_val, max_display=10, show=False)
```

The resulting plot, ordered by mean absolute SHAP value:

```
logins_last_30d                  0.91
days_since_last_login            0.74
open_support_tickets_last_90d    0.18
SeatCount                        0.11
MonthlyRevenue                   0.09
logins_last_90d                  0.07
PlanTier_Enterprise               0.04
Industry_SaaS                     0.02
...
```

`logins_last_30d` and `days_since_last_login` together carry more weight than every remaining feature combined.

## Step 4 -- Explain one specific account

```python
account_idx = X_val.index.get_loc(X_val["AccountId"].eq(482193).idxmax())

shap.force_plot(
    explainer.expected_value,
    shap_values[account_idx],
    X_val.iloc[account_idx],
)
```

For account 482193 -- flagged at 0.89 predicted churn risk -- the force plot shows the prediction pushed almost entirely above the baseline by two bars: a near-zero `logins_last_30d` and a `days_since_last_login` well past 20 days. `open_support_tickets_last_90d` and `SeatCount` contribute, but barely, compared to the two login-recency features.

## Step 5 -- Write up the finding for Dana Okafor and Tom Bellamy

```
MODEL EXPLAINABILITY SUMMARY -- Everpeak Churn Risk Model v1

The model's predictions are driven overwhelmingly by recent login activity:
logins_last_30d and days_since_last_login together account for the large
majority of each prediction's SHAP contribution. This tracks with the
intuitive pattern Customer Success already watches for -- accounts that
stop logging in are accounts that are about to churn.
```

The summary is accurate about what the model learned and reads as good news. It is filed alongside the 0.98 AUC as supporting evidence that the model is sound. Lesson 15 is where this exact finding gets looked at again, from a different angle.

## Step 6 -- Dana Okafor and Tom Bellamy sign off on the explanation

Dana Okafor reviews the summary plot in the next pipeline sync and calls it "exactly the story we'd expect to see" -- accounts that stop engaging are accounts that leave. Tom Bellamy's only question is whether the model is more confident about enterprise accounts than smaller ones, since that would change how his team prioritizes outreach. The SHAP ranking answers it without anyone having to dig further: `PlanTier_Enterprise` and `PlanTier_Pro` barely register next to `logins_last_30d` and `days_since_last_login`, so the model is reading engagement drop-off roughly the same way across every segment, regardless of account size or plan.

That answer satisfies the room. Nobody follows up by asking a different, harder question: could `logins_last_30d` be measuring something the model would never actually have access to when scoring a real, still-active account? There's no reason to ask it yet -- the model is explainable, the explanation is intuitive, and the offline number is excellent. That question doesn't get asked until Lesson 15, when the production numbers stop matching it.

```python
shap.summary_plot(shap_values, X_val, max_display=10, show=False)
plt.savefig("reports/shap_summary_v1.png", bbox_inches="tight", dpi=150)
```

Force plot on a flagged account confirms the same two features drive nearly the entire prediction. Interpreted as a legitimate engagement-decline signal for now; no leakage check run against it yet.

lessons.title: Deploying the Scoring Pipeline to Azure ML
lessons.summary: Grace Lindqvist takes the explained model live on a weekly Azure ML Batch Endpoint.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With the model trained, explained, and signed off, Grace Lindqvist takes it from a notebook to something Tom Bellamy's Renewals team can actually rely on every week. This lesson registers the LightGBM model as a versioned asset in Azure ML, builds a batch endpoint around a scoring script that reads each account's current feature values from `EVERPEAK_PROD`, and schedules the whole pipeline to run automatically every Monday morning, writing results to a new `dbo.ChurnRiskScores` table.

Nothing about the model itself changes here -- this lesson is purely the deployment plumbing that turns a one-off training run into a recurring production system. The endpoint goes live, the first weekly run completes cleanly, scores land in SQL Server exactly where Renewals expects them, and the team closes the lesson feeling good about shipping a model that tested at 0.98 AUC. No one has a reason yet to look twice at how the batch job computes its features relative to today, instead of relative to some future date it can't possibly know.
lessons.explainSimple: Think about the difference between a chef who cooks you one great meal to prove they can, and a kitchen that cooks the same meal correctly every single day without the chef standing there. This lesson builds that kitchen. The model already proved it works -- now it needs to run itself, automatically, once a week, reading today's information and writing today's answer to a place everyone already knows to check. Nobody's tasting the food differently this week than they did last week. It's the exact same recipe. It just runs on its own now.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Azure ML's model registry and batch endpoint are the standard path from a trained artifact to a recurring, auditable production job: register the model once as a versioned asset, define an endpoint and deployment pointing at a scoring script with `init()` and `run()` entry points, and attach a schedule so the batch job executes without manual triggering. The scoring script here pulls each account's current feature values -- computed as of the run date, because that's the only date a production job ever has -- scores them with the registered model, and writes `AccountId`, `ScoreDate`, and `ChurnRiskScore` to `dbo.ChurnRiskScores`.

This is a structurally important but easy-to-miss detail: a batch job scoring live accounts has no access to any account's future `ChurnDate`, by definition -- it's scoring accounts precisely because their outcome isn't known yet. Whatever features the training pipeline used, the production scoring script can only ever compute them relative to the actual calendar date it runs on. That constraint is simply inherent to deployment; it isn't treated as a red flag about how training itself computed those same features. The gap between what training assumed and what production can actually do doesn't surface until a few weeks of real scores come back.

```python
ws = Workspace.get(
    name="everpeak-ml-workspace",
    subscription_id=AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID,
    resource_group="everpeak-data-science-rg",

print(ws.name, ws.compute_targets.keys())
# dict_keys(['batch-cluster', 'training-cluster'])
```

## Step 2 -- Register the model in Azure ML

```python
from azureml.core import Workspace, Model

ws = Workspace.from_config()

churn_model = Model.register(
    workspace=ws,
    model_path="models/lightgbm_churn_v1.pkl",
    model_name="everpeak-churn-risk-lgbm",
    description="LightGBM churn risk model. Offline validation AUC 0.98.",
    tags={"owner": "felix.granger", "algorithm": "lightgbm"},
)
print(churn_model.name, churn_model.version)
```

## Step 3 -- Write the scoring script

```python
# scoring/score.py
import joblib
import pandas as pd
import pyodbc

FEATURE_COLS = [
    "logins_last_30d", "logins_last_90d", "days_since_last_login",
    "open_support_tickets_last_90d", "SeatCount", "MonthlyRevenue",
]

def init():
    global model
    model = joblib.load("everpeak-churn-risk-lgbm/model.pkl")

def run(mini_batch):
    outputs = []
    for batch_file in mini_batch:
        df = pd.read_parquet(batch_file)  # one row per AccountId, features as of today
        df["ChurnRiskScore"] = model.predict_proba(df[FEATURE_COLS])[:, 1]
        df["ScoreDate"] = pd.Timestamp.today().normalize()
        write_scores(df[["AccountId", "ScoreDate", "ChurnRiskScore"]])
        outputs.append(df)
    return pd.concat(outputs)

def write_scores(df):
    conn = pyodbc.connect(EVERPEAK_PROD_CONN_STR)
    cursor = conn.cursor()
    for _, row in df.iterrows():
        cursor.execute(
            "INSERT INTO dbo.ChurnRiskScores (AccountId, ScoreDate, ChurnRiskScore, ModelVersion) "
            "VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)",
            row.AccountId, row.ScoreDate, row.ChurnRiskScore, "everpeak-churn-risk-lgbm:1",
        )
    conn.commit()
```

## Step 4 -- Test the scoring script against a handful of real accounts before deploying it

```python
import pandas as pd

sample_batch = pd.read_parquet("data/sample_accounts_today.parquet")  # 20 real accounts, current features
import scoring.score as score

score.init()
result = score.run(["data/sample_accounts_today.parquet"])
print(result[["AccountId", "ChurnRiskScore"]].head())
```

Running the script locally against a small, real sample before it ever touches the batch cluster catches the obvious failure modes -- a missing feature column, a schema mismatch against `EVERPEAK_PROD`, a connection string pointed at the wrong environment -- while they're still cheap to fix.

## Step 5 -- Create the destination table

```sql
CREATE TABLE dbo.ChurnRiskScores (
    AccountId      INT          NOT NULL,
    ScoreDate      DATE         NOT NULL,
    ChurnRiskScore FLOAT        NOT NULL,
    ModelVersion   VARCHAR(50)  NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT PK_ChurnRiskScores PRIMARY KEY (AccountId, ScoreDate)
);
```

## Step 6 -- Create the batch endpoint and deployment

lessons.title: The Model That Looked Too Good to Be True
lessons.summary: Weeks of real scores later, Felix and Grace trace the 0.98 AUC back to a leak -- real AUC is 0.74.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
A few weeks of real weekly scoring go by. Tom Bellamy's team starts comparing the risk scores in `dbo.ChurnRiskScores` against which accounts actually renew and which don't, and the pattern isn't there -- plenty of accounts flagged high-risk renew without incident, and some low-scored accounts churn anyway. A model that tested at 0.98 AUC offline should not look this unremarkable in production.

Felix Granger and Grace Lindqvist investigate, and the trail leads straight back to Lesson 13's SHAP plot: why did the model lean so overwhelmingly on just `logins_last_30d` and `days_since_last_login`? Pulling the original training SQL answers it. Those two features were computed relative to `COALESCE(ChurnDate, CURRENT_DATE)` -- for a churned account, that anchor point is the day it already left, not any date available 90 days beforehand. The batch endpoint from Lesson 14 can only ever compute the same features relative to today, because it has no future knowledge of which accounts will later churn; it was never capable of reproducing what training saw. Running an honest, time-consistent backtest -- scoring accounts exactly the way production does, using only data available as of a fixed historical date -- puts the real AUC at approximately 0.74. The gap between 0.98 and 0.74 is the size of the leak. The lesson ends there: diagnosed, not yet fixed.
lessons.explainSimple: Imagine a weather forecaster who claims 98% accuracy, and it turns out the way they tested that number was by checking their rain forecast against what the sky already looked like the moment it started raining -- not against what they actually knew the day before. Of course that looks almost perfectly accurate. It isn't really a forecast at all; it's just describing the rain after it's already falling. Once someone checks the forecaster's real predictions against what they genuinely knew in advance, the accuracy drops a lot -- not because the forecaster got worse, but because the first number was never honest in the first place.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The investigation here follows the mismatch backward rather than forward: production results don't match offline claims, so the offline evaluation methodology itself becomes the suspect, not the model's architecture or hyperparameters. Re-examining Lesson 13's SHAP output in this light reframes it entirely -- a model whose predictions are carried almost entirely by two features is also exactly what a leaked feature looks like, because a leaked feature correlates with the label far more strongly than any legitimate signal could.

The root cause, once found, is a classic temporal leak: `logins_last_30d` and `days_since_last_login` were computed in the training pipeline using `COALESCE(ChurnDate, CURRENT_DATE)` as the window anchor instead of a single `OBSERVATION_DATE` shared by every row. For a row representing a churned account, that anchor is the account's own churn date -- so `logins_last_30d` measures login activity in the 30 days immediately before the account left, which is almost always near zero, because customers who are about to leave largely stop logging in first. The feature isn't an early-warning signal computed from information available 90 days out; it's a near-restatement of the outcome itself, computed with information that was never available at the time a real prediction would need to be made.

The diagnostic test that confirms it is a time-consistent backtest: pick a historical `OBSERVATION_DATE`, compute every feature using only data timestamped before it, score with the existing model, and compare against the real outcome in the 90 days that followed. That honest evaluation returns an AUC of approximately 0.74 -- a reasonable, unremarkable score for a real early-warning model, and the actual ceiling the 0.98 number was always masking.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Tom Bellamy's team flags it first

Three weeks into the weekly batch run, Tom Bellamy brings a simple observation to the pipeline sync: several accounts his team called "obviously fine" during renewal conversations are sitting at 0.85+ risk scores in `dbo.ChurnRiskScores`, and a few accounts that did quietly churn were scored low the week before. Individually, misses like this would be expected from any real model -- but the pattern feels more random than a 0.98 AUC model should ever look.

## Step 2 -- Confirm the mismatch is real

```sql
SELECT
    crs.AccountId,
    crs.ChurnRiskScore,
    crs.ScoreDate,
    CASE WHEN a.ChurnDate BETWEEN crs.ScoreDate AND DATEADD(day, 90, crs.ScoreDate)
         THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS actually_churned_within_90d
FROM dbo.ChurnRiskScores crs
JOIN dbo.Accounts a ON a.AccountId = crs.AccountId
WHERE crs.ScoreDate <= DATEADD(day, -90, CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE));
```

Across several weeks of resolved scores, high-risk accounts churn at only a modestly higher rate than low-risk accounts -- nothing close to what a 0.98 AUC model should produce.

## Step 3 -- Go back to the Lesson 13 SHAP finding

`logins_last_30d` and `days_since_last_login` carried the overwhelming majority of the model's predictive weight. In isolation that looked like a clean, intuitive story. Next to a production model that isn't performing, it looks like something else: a model over-relying on two features is also what a leak looks like.

## Step 4 -- Pull the original training feature SQL

```sql
-- The training-time feature query, as originally written
SELECT
    a.AccountId,
    COALESCE(a.ChurnDate, CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE)) AS anchor_date,
    (
      SELECT COUNT(*) FROM dbo.UsageEvents u
      WHERE u.AccountId = a.AccountId
        AND u.EventTimestamp >= DATEADD(day, -30, COALESCE(a.ChurnDate, CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE)))
        AND u.EventTimestamp <  COALESCE(a.ChurnDate, CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE))
    ) AS logins_last_30d,
    DATEDIFF(day,
      (SELECT MAX(u2.EventTimestamp) FROM dbo.UsageEvents u2
       WHERE u2.AccountId = a.AccountId
         AND u2.EventTimestamp < COALESCE(a.ChurnDate, CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE))),
      COALESCE(a.ChurnDate, CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE))
    ) AS days_since_last_login
FROM dbo.Accounts a;
```

For a churned account, `anchor_date` is its own `ChurnDate` -- `logins_last_30d` counts logins in the 30 days right before it left, which is almost always near-zero. Production, scoring live accounts, has no `ChurnDate` to anchor on and can only ever use today.

## Step 5 -- Run the honest, time-consistent backtest

```python
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

backtest_observation_date = "2026-01-15"  # far enough in the past that the 90-day outcome is already known

df_backtest = build_feature_snapshot(observation_date=backtest_observation_date)
df_backtest["y_true"] = label_90d_forward(df_backtest, backtest_observation_date)

X_backtest = df_backtest[feature_cols]
y_pred = model.predict_proba(X_backtest)[:, 1]

honest_auc = roc_auc_score(df_backtest["y_true"], y_pred)
print(f"Honest time-consistent backtest AUC: {honest_auc:.2f}")
# Honest time-consistent backtest AUC: 0.74
```

## Step 6 -- Name the finding precisely

```
DIAGNOSIS: logins_last_30d and days_since_last_login were computed at
training time relative to COALESCE(ChurnDate, CURRENT_DATE). For churned
accounts, this anchors the window to the account's own churn date -- future
information unavailable at any real prediction time. Production can only
ever anchor to the actual run date, so it was never capable of reproducing
the offline result.

Offline (leaked) AUC: 0.98
Honest time-consistent backtest AUC: 0.74

Not yet fixed. Lesson 16 rebuilds the features correctly.
```

Grace Lindqvist's reaction in the writeup thread is the one that sticks: "the batch endpoint was never broken -- it was doing exactly what we built it to do. It just couldn't do the thing training was secretly relying on." Felix shares the diagnosis with Dana Okafor and Tom Bellamy the same day, before a fix exists, because an honest 0.74 they understand is worth more than a 0.98 they don't.

A time-consistent backtest confirms the real AUC was always about 0.74. Not yet fixed.

lessons.title: Finding and Fixing the Leakage
lessons.summary: Trailing-window features get rebuilt on one fixed OBSERVATION_DATE; retrained model lands at a real 0.79 AUC.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Lesson 15 diagnosed exactly what went wrong: `logins_last_30d` and `days_since_last_login` were anchored to `COALESCE(ChurnDate, CURRENT_DATE)` instead of a fixed point every row shared, leaking future information into training. This lesson fixes it at the source. Every trailing-window feature -- `logins_last_30d`, `logins_last_90d`, `open_support_tickets_last_90d`, and `days_since_last_login` -- gets redefined relative to a single, fixed `OBSERVATION_DATE` per training row, with `dbo.UsageEvents` and `dbo.SupportTickets` strictly excluded past that date. The label is computed independently, from a separate forward-looking window: churn strictly after `OBSERVATION_DATE` and within the following 90 days.

With the corrected features in place, LightGBM gets retrained from scratch, and the same honest, time-consistent backtest from Lesson 15 runs again -- this time against a model that was never given information it shouldn't have had. The corrected AUC lands at approximately 0.79: a real, modest, believable improvement over the 0.74 honest baseline, nowhere near the fake 0.98, and the number the rest of this series treats as the model's actual standing performance. The lesson closes with a process change -- a standing review rule -- so this exact class of bug can't slip through again unnoticed.
lessons.explainSimple: Going back to the weather forecaster: the fix isn't to throw out the forecasting method, it's to only ever let the forecaster use information that was actually available the day before, every single time, with no exceptions -- never information from the moment it started raining. Once that rule is enforced everywhere in how the forecast is built, and the forecaster is retrained on forecasts made the honest way, the accuracy settles at a real, believable number -- lower than the fake 98%, but actually true, and actually useful. That's the number everyone can trust going forward.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The fix enforces a single invariant across every trailing-window feature: one `OBSERVATION_DATE` per training row, computed identically regardless of whether that row's account eventually churns, with all source data timestamped after `OBSERVATION_DATE` strictly excluded from the feature computation. The label is deliberately computed from a disjoint window -- `(OBSERVATION_DATE, OBSERVATION_DATE + 90 days]` -- so there is no shared computation path between what the model sees as input and what it's being asked to predict.

In practice this means generating multiple historical snapshots per account (one training row per account per chosen `OBSERVATION_DATE`), each with features built only from `dbo.UsageEvents` and `dbo.SupportTickets` rows at or before that date, and a label resolved independently using `dbo.Accounts.ChurnDate`. Retraining LightGBM on this corrected dataset and re-running the identical time-consistent backtest from Lesson 15 produces an AUC of approximately 0.79 -- meaningfully above the 0.74 honest baseline the unmodified model actually achieved, and credible precisely because the improvement is modest rather than dramatic. This 0.79 figure becomes the model's real, standing validated performance for every later lesson in this series.

The closing process change matters as much as the fix itself: a standing review rule requiring that every trailing-window feature's SQL or pandas logic be checked against one question before a model ships -- would this value be identical for an active account and a to-be-churned account observed at the same point in time? A feature that fails that test is a leak candidate by construction, independent of how good its SHAP ranking looks.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Define the corrected feature query, anchored on one fixed date

```sql
DECLARE @ObservationDate DATE = '2026-04-01';

SELECT
    a.AccountId,
    @ObservationDate AS observation_date,
    CASE WHEN a.ChurnDate > @ObservationDate
              AND a.ChurnDate <= DATEADD(day, 90, @ObservationDate)
         THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS label_churned_90d,

    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM dbo.UsageEvents u
     WHERE u.AccountId = a.AccountId
       AND u.EventTimestamp >= DATEADD(day, -30, @ObservationDate)
       AND u.EventTimestamp <  @ObservationDate
    ) AS logins_last_30d,

    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM dbo.UsageEvents u
     WHERE u.AccountId = a.AccountId
       AND u.EventTimestamp >= DATEADD(day, -90, @ObservationDate)
       AND u.EventTimestamp <  @ObservationDate
    ) AS logins_last_90d,

    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM dbo.SupportTickets t
     WHERE t.AccountId = a.AccountId
       AND t.OpenedDate >= DATEADD(day, -90, @ObservationDate)
       AND t.OpenedDate <  @ObservationDate
       AND (t.ClosedDate IS NULL OR t.ClosedDate >= @ObservationDate)
    ) AS open_support_tickets_last_90d,

    DATEDIFF(day,
      (SELECT MAX(u2.EventTimestamp) FROM dbo.UsageEvents u2
       WHERE u2.AccountId = a.AccountId
         AND u2.EventTimestamp < @ObservationDate),
      @ObservationDate
    ) AS days_since_last_login
FROM dbo.Accounts a
WHERE a.ContractStartDate <= @ObservationDate
  AND (a.ChurnDate IS NULL OR a.ChurnDate > @ObservationDate);
```

Every feature stops strictly before `@ObservationDate`. The label looks only in the window after it. Nothing shares a computation path with anything else.

## Step 2 -- Generate multiple historical snapshots, not just one

```python
observation_dates = pd.date_range("2025-01-01", "2026-01-01", freq="MS")

frames = []
for obs_date in observation_dates:
    frames.append(build_feature_snapshot(observation_date=obs_date.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")))

training_df = pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True)
print(training_df.shape)
```

Each account contributes one row per monthly snapshot it was active for, each computed against that snapshot's own fixed `OBSERVATION_DATE` -- never today's date, never `ChurnDate`.

## Step 3 -- Confirm the leak test on the new features

```python
# Sanity check: feature values must not depend on future churn status
active_sample = training_df[training_df["label_churned_90d"] == 0].sample(500, random_state=1)
churned_sample = training_df[training_df["label_churned_90d"] == 1].sample(500, random_state=1)

print(active_sample["logins_last_30d"].describe())
print(churned_sample["logins_last_30d"].describe())
# Distributions now overlap meaningfully -- no longer near-zero for every churned row
```

## Step 4 -- Retrain LightGBM on the corrected data

```python
import lightgbm as lgb
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X = training_df[feature_cols]
y = training_df["label_churned_90d"]

X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=1, stratify=y)

model_v2 = lgb.LGBMClassifier(n_estimators=300, learning_rate=0.05, random_state=1)
model_v2.fit(X_train, y_train)

joblib.dump(model_v2, "models/lightgbm_churn_v2.pkl")
```

## Step 5 -- Re-run the exact same honest backtest from Lesson 15

```python
backtest_observation_date = "2026-01-15"

df_backtest = build_feature_snapshot(observation_date=backtest_observation_date)
df_backtest["y_true"] = label_90d_forward(df_backtest, backtest_observation_date)

y_pred_v2 = model_v2.predict_proba(df_backtest[feature_cols])[:, 1]
honest_auc_v2 = roc_auc_score(df_backtest["y_true"], y_pred_v2)

print(f"Corrected model, honest backtest AUC: {honest_auc_v2:.2f}")
# Corrected model, honest backtest AUC: 0.79
```

0.79 against a 0.74 honest baseline -- a real, modest lift, and the number the rest of this project treats as the model's actual performance.

## Step 6 -- Register the corrected model and retire the leaked one

```python
Model.register(
    workspace=ws,
    model_path="models/lightgbm_churn_v2.pkl",
    model_name="everpeak-churn-risk-lgbm",
    description="LightGBM churn risk model v2. Features rebuilt on fixed OBSERVATION_DATE. Honest backtest AUC 0.79.",
    tags={"owner": "felix.granger", "supersedes": "v1 (leaked, offline 0.98 / honest 0.74)"},
)
```

The Lesson 14 batch deployment gets pointed at this new version in a later lesson.

## Step 7 -- Write the process rule down

```
ROOT CAUSE: logins_last_30d and days_since_last_login were computed at
training time relative to COALESCE(ChurnDate, CURRENT_DATE) instead of a
fixed OBSERVATION_DATE. This leaked future information for churned accounts
and produced a fake 0.98 offline AUC against a real 0.74.

FIX: every trailing-window feature rebuilt relative to one fixed
OBSERVATION_DATE per row, with source data after that date strictly
excluded. Retrained model's honest backtest AUC: 0.79.

STANDING RULE: before any model ships, every trailing-window feature's
SQL or pandas logic must be checked against one question -- would this
value be identical for an active account and a to-be-churned account,
observed at the same point in time? If the answer is no, the feature is a
leak candidate regardless of how strong its SHAP ranking looks.
```

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Rebuilt logins_last_30d, logins_last_90d, open_support_tickets_last_90d, and days_since_last_login against a single fixed OBSERVATION_DATE per training row, excluding all UsageEvents/SupportTickets after that date, with the label computed from an independent forward window. Retrained LightGBM (model_v2), re-ran the Lesson 15 honest backtest, confirmed AUC of 0.79 against the 0.74 honest baseline. Registered v2 in Azure ML; added a standing feature-review rule to prevent recurrence.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've fixed the root cause behind the gap we found -- the model now only ever sees information it would genuinely have at prediction time. We retrained it and re-tested it honestly, and it now shows a real, modest improvement over the honest baseline we measured last time. We've also put a permanent check in place so this specific type of mistake gets caught before any future model ships.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've corrected the issue behind the model's inflated test score. The retrained model now shows real, verified improvement over the honest baseline -- a believable result we can actually stand behind -- and we've added a standing review step to our process so this kind of problem is caught automatically before any model goes live going forward.

lessons.title: Presenting the Real Numbers to Leadership, Leakage Included
lessons.summary: Felix Granger presents the corrected churn model to Dana Okafor, Tom Bellamy, and leadership -- stating the real ~0.79 AUC plainly and walking through how the leakage bug was found and fixed, framed as the validation process working.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
This is the moment the churn-risk project has been building toward: Felix Granger stands in front of Dana Okafor, Tom Bellamy, and Everpeak's broader leadership and presents the finished, corrected model -- not the one that once scored an eye-catching 0.98 AUC, but the one that actually works in production, with a real, honestly-measured AUC of about 0.79. Getting to this room means walking through the leakage bug plainly: two features, `logins_last_30d` and `days_since_last_login`, were quietly computed off each account's own `ChurnDate` instead of a fixed `OBSERVATION_DATE`, which let the model see a few weeks into a churned account's future before predicting its past. SHAP had already shown those two features dominating every prediction -- the tell, in hindsight, that something was wrong before anyone acted on it.

The skill in this video isn't technical. It's choosing to open a leadership meeting with a number that's lower than the one everyone got excited about three months ago, and explaining why that's actually the good number -- the one that will still be true in production six months from now, because it's the one the team found by testing the model the way production actually sees data, not the one that looked best on a slide.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a student who takes a practice test with the answer key accidentally tucked inside the test booklet. They score 98%, everyone celebrates, and then they sit the real exam -- without the answer key -- and barely pass. The practice score was never a lie exactly, it was just measuring the wrong thing: how well the student could copy an answer that was sitting right there, not how well they actually knew the material.

That's almost exactly what happened with Everpeak's first churn model. It scored an eye-popping 98 out of 100 in testing, because two of its clues were secretly measuring something that only exists after an account has already churned -- like grading the practice test with the answer key left in. Once that mistake got fixed and the model was tested fairly, honestly, the way it would actually be used, its real score came out to about 79 out of 100. That's not a failure. That's the team finding and removing the answer key before handing the test to someone who was actually going to rely on the score.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A leadership presentation about a machine learning model succeeds or fails on one decision: whether the person presenting it treats the validated metric as the deliverable, or treats the story around that metric as the deliverable. Felix's presentation here does the former. The headline number is 0.79 AUC on a time-consistent backtest -- scoring, for every historical account, with only the features that would have actually been knowable as of a fixed `OBSERVATION_DATE`, never anything derived from data that came after it. That discipline is what makes 0.79 a number leadership can actually plan around, instead of a number that will quietly erode the first time someone compares a live batch-scoring run against the original offline claim.

Naming the leakage bug specifically, rather than alluding to "some early modeling issues," matters for the same reason an honest incident retrospective always matters: a named, mechanistic explanation is what lets the room trust the fix, not just the apology. `logins_last_30d` and `days_since_last_login`, as originally built, used each account's own churn date as the anchor for a trailing window -- which meant a churned account's "recent activity" features were effectively measuring the weeks right before it went silent, information that is simply unavailable at actual scoring time for an account that hasn't churned yet. SHAP's feature-importance ranking had already flagged these two features as overwhelmingly dominant contributors well before anyone traced the mechanism -- in hindsight, a model leaning that hard on two features is itself a signal worth investigating, not just a sign the model found something powerful.

The reframe that makes this presentation land is simple and honest: catching this before it shipped to Tom Bellamy's team at full trust, through the team's own validation discipline rather than a customer complaint or a quarter of bad renewal decisions, is the process working exactly as it should.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Open with what's actually being presented, before the number

Remind the room of the real goal: a 90-day-ahead churn risk score for every one of Everpeak's roughly 40,000 paying accounts, scored weekly, feeding Tom Bellamy's Renewals team with both a risk level and a reason. That's the deliverable. Everything else in this meeting is about how much that score can actually be trusted.

## Step 2 -- State the real number plainly, first

```
MODEL PERFORMANCE -- WHAT THIS ROOM SHOULD BELIEVE

Original offline claim:      AUC ~0.98  (invalid -- caused by leakage)
Honest time-consistent test: AUC ~0.74  (the ORIGINAL model's real score)
Corrected model, in production: AUC ~0.79  (real, validated, standing)
```

Say the 0.79 first, not last. Burying it at the end of a slide deck under a wall of caveats reads as reluctance; leading with it reads as confidence in a number that's actually been earned.

## Step 3 -- Name the leakage bug by its exact mechanism

```
YOU: Our first trained model scored an offline AUC of 0.98. That
     number was wrong -- not fabricated, wrong. Two features,
     logins_last_30d and days_since_last_login, were computed using
     each account's own churn date as the anchor for a trailing
     window instead of one fixed observation date. For an account
     that already churned, "logins in the last 30 days" ends up
     measuring activity right around when it stopped using the
     product -- which is nearly the same information as the label
     we were trying to predict.
```

## Step 4 -- Explain why SHAP was the tell, not the discovery

SHAP explainability, built earlier in this project, had already shown these same two features dominating almost every prediction. Say this plainly: "A model leaning that hard on two features was itself worth investigating before we trusted the number -- SHAP showed us where to look before we knew why."

## Step 5 -- State the fix and the honest backtest that followed

```
FIX: every trailing-window feature redefined relative to one fixed
     OBSERVATION_DATE per training row, with nothing computed from
     data after that date -- including logins_last_30d and
     days_since_last_login
RESULT: an honest, time-consistent backtest -- scoring the way
     production actually sees data -- puts the corrected model at
     AUC ~0.79. That is the real, standing number this team is
     accountable for going forward.
```

## Step 6 -- Frame the good news correctly

The right frame isn't "we made a mistake and fixed it," it's "our own validation process caught this before it ever reached Tom's team at full trust." Nobody's renewal decisions were ever made against the 0.98 number in production -- the gap was found in offline validation, before the batch endpoint ever shipped a score anyone acted on.

## Step 7 -- Rehearse the hard question

```
Q: How do we know there isn't another leakage bug like this
   somewhere else in the pipeline?
A: We don't know that with certainty -- nobody legitimately can.
   What changed is that every new feature now gets checked against
   a fixed observation date before it's trusted, and SHAP review is
   now a standing step in every model review, not a one-time audit.
```

## Step 8 -- Close by asking for explicit sign-off

Ask Dana and Tom directly to confirm that 0.79 AUC, not 0.98, is the number they're planning around for this quarter's renewal process -- and that they understand the honest backtest methodology behind it well enough to defend it if someone asks them where it came from.

Framed the honest 0.74 backtest on the original model as proof the validation process works, not as a confession.
