lessons.title: From Risk Score to Retention Action
lessons.summary: Translating dbo.ChurnRiskScores and its SHAP explanations into Tom Bellamy's team's actual weekly workflow -- what a flagged account's reason looks like in practice, and how a rep decides what to do with it.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With the corrected model presented and trusted, this video follows the risk score the rest of the way -- out of `dbo.ChurnRiskScores` and into an actual Tuesday morning on Tom Bellamy's Renewals team. Every week, the Azure ML Batch Endpoint job scores all ~40,000 accounts and writes each account's `AccountId`, `ScoreDate`, `ChurnRiskScore` (the raw probability), and `ModelVersion` into that table -- the reproducible core the deployment already produces. This lesson is about the layer built on top of that raw number: a derived risk tier computed by a simple score-threshold rule, and a short, plain-language explanation generated from the same SHAP values built earlier in this project, applied per flagged account by the same weekly batch job and written to a companion table, `dbo.ChurnRiskExplanations`. This lesson is about what a rep actually sees when they open that list, how a flagged account's reason reads in plain language -- not a SHAP value, a sentence -- and what a rep is expected to do with that information once they have it.

It also names a real, not-yet-built idea for where this naturally goes next: a generative-AI assistant that drafts a personalized outreach email grounded in the specific SHAP reasons for a flagged account, for a human rep to review, edit, and send -- never auto-sent. That idea gets named honestly as a V2 concept here, consistent with what this platform's generative-AI course already teaches, not claimed as something already live.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a weather app that doesn't just say "70% chance of rain" but also says why: "clouds moving in from the west, humidity rising fast." That second part is what actually helps you decide whether to carry an umbrella -- a number alone tells you less than a number plus a reason.

That's exactly what Tom Bellamy's team gets every week. It's not just a list of account names with a risk number next to them -- each flagged account comes with a plain-language reason, built from the same SHAP explanations the data science team already trusts: something like "usage down 60% over the last 90 days, and 2 open support tickets." A rep reads that sentence and immediately knows whether to make a phone call about a technical problem or a renewal conversation about adoption -- the number alone would never have told them that.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The handoff from a risk score to a usable workflow is where most churn-modeling projects quietly fail, even when the model itself is sound -- a bare probability with no explanation just produces a long, undifferentiated list that a Renewals team either ignores or works through by gut feeling, which defeats the purpose of building the model at all. `dbo.ChurnRiskScores` stores exactly what the batch endpoint needs to store to stay reproducible: `AccountId`, `ScoreDate`, the raw `ChurnRiskScore` probability, and the `ModelVersion` that produced it. The design choice that makes this project actually useful to Tom's team is the layer built on top of that raw table -- a derived risk tier (High/Medium/Low) computed by a simple score-threshold rule, and a short, plain-language explanation generated from the same SHAP values already computed earlier in this project, applied per account at scoring time and written to `dbo.ChurnRiskExplanations` -- not a raw feature-contribution table. "Usage down 60% over 90 days, 2 open support tickets" is something Tom's reps can act on in the time it takes to glance at a weekly report; a SHAP waterfall plot is not.

That explanation does real triage work before a rep even picks up the phone. An account flagged primarily for declining usage calls for a very different conversation -- adoption, training, a check-in on whether the product still fits their workflow -- than one flagged primarily for open support tickets, which calls for an escalation to make sure those tickets actually get resolved before any renewal conversation happens. The score tells a rep *who* to look at first; the explanation tells them *what kind of conversation* to have.

The generative-AI drafting idea belongs here specifically because it's the next logical extension of exactly this pattern, not a separate feature: an LLM given the same SHAP-based reason already shown to the rep, prompted to draft a short, personalized outreach email grounded in that reason, with a human rep required to read, edit, and send it -- never auto-sent. Naming it honestly as a real, concrete V2 idea, not yet built, keeps today's presentation to Tom's team accurate about what exists right now.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Walk the weekly cycle end to end

```
MONDAY NIGHT:  Azure ML Batch Endpoint scores all ~40,000 accounts,
               writing AccountId, ScoreDate, ChurnRiskScore (the raw
               probability), and ModelVersion into dbo.ChurnRiskScores.
               The same run also computes a short SHAP-based
               explanation for every account that scores above the
               Medium threshold, and writes it to a companion table,
               dbo.ChurnRiskExplanations (AccountId, ScoreDate,
               ExplanationText).
TUESDAY AM:    Tom Bellamy's team opens the week's High-risk list --
               typically a few hundred accounts out of ~40,000 --
               ranked by ChurnRiskScore, with a reason attached
```

The weekly cadence matters on its own: a 90-day-ahead prediction doesn't need to be scored daily, and weekly is frequent enough to catch a meaningfully changing account before the next renewal cycle without generating noise nobody can act on.

## Step 2 -- Show what a rep actually sees

```sql
SELECT
    s.AccountId,
    a.AccountName,
    s.ChurnRiskScore,
    CASE WHEN s.ChurnRiskScore >= 0.75 THEN 'High'
         WHEN s.ChurnRiskScore >= 0.45 THEN 'Medium'
         ELSE 'Low' END AS RiskTier,
    e.ExplanationText
FROM dbo.ChurnRiskScores s
JOIN dbo.Accounts a ON a.AccountId = s.AccountId
LEFT JOIN dbo.ChurnRiskExplanations e
    ON e.AccountId = s.AccountId AND e.ScoreDate = s.ScoreDate
WHERE s.ScoreDate = (SELECT MAX(ScoreDate) FROM dbo.ChurnRiskScores)
ORDER BY s.ChurnRiskScore DESC;
```

```
AccountId: 48213   RiskTier: High   ChurnRiskScore: 0.87
ExplanationText: "Usage down 62% over the last 90 days; 2 open support
                 tickets (1 unresolved 14+ days)"
```

`ExplanationText` is built from the top SHAP contributors for that specific account -- the same explainer already used earlier in this project, loaded once in the batch job's `init()` and applied per flagged account in `run()`, right alongside the scoring itself. It's converted from feature names and values into a sentence a rep can read in two seconds -- not a raw SHAP plot and not a generic "high risk" label with no reason attached. The risk tier itself is a derived business rule, not a separately-maintained value, so a threshold change never has to be backfilled into history.

## Step 3 -- Give reps an actual decision rule, not just a list

```
IF explanation leads with USAGE DECLINE:
    -> adoption/check-in conversation: is the product still fitting
       their workflow, does a team need re-training, has a champion
       left the account
IF explanation leads with OPEN SUPPORT TICKETS:
    -> escalate the ticket first, THEN have the renewal conversation
       -- a renewal call before the actual problem is fixed usually
       makes things worse, not better
IF explanation shows BOTH:
    -> treat as the week's highest priority; loop in a CSM, not just
       a renewals rep
```

This is the actual value SHAP adds over a bare score: it tells a rep which of two very different conversations to have, not just who to call first.

## Step 4 -- Name what this workflow does NOT do

No account gets an automated email, discount, or outreach triggered by this score alone. Every action on a flagged account is still a human decision and a human email or call. That's a deliberate V1 boundary, not a missing feature -- a wrong automated message to a frustrated customer does more damage than a slightly-delayed human one.

## Step 5 -- Name the real V2 idea, honestly, as not yet built

```
NOT YET BUILT -- A CONCRETE V2 IDEA:
An LLM drafts a short, personalized outreach email for a flagged
account, grounded specifically in that account's SHAP-based reason
(e.g., referencing the usage decline or the open ticket by name) --
never auto-sent. A human rep reads it, edits it, and decides whether
to send it at all. This is a natural extension of generative AI
grounded in real account data -- but it does not exist in this
system today.
```

## Step 6 -- Close the loop: how feedback should eventually improve the model

Right now, whether a rep's outreach to a flagged account actually worked -- did the account renew, did usage recover -- isn't fed back into the model in any structured way. Flag this honestly as a gap worth closing eventually: a rep's own read on an account carries real signal that the model currently never learns from.

Gave reps a concrete decision rule keyed off whether the explanation leads with usage decline, open tickets, or both, and drew a hard line that no outreach is automated -- every action stays a human email or call. Named the generative-AI drafting idea as a concrete, not-yet-built V2 concept.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Documented exactly how Tom's team uses the risk score day to day: a weekly High-risk list with a plain-English reason attached to every account, and a clear rule for what kind of conversation each type of flag calls for. Confirmed with Tom that no automated outreach exists today -- every action is still a human decision -- and logged the LLM-drafted-email idea as a named V2 candidate, not a current feature.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The risk score isn't just a number on a list -- every flagged account comes with a plain-English reason a rep can act on immediately, like 'usage down 60%, two open tickets.' Reaching out to a customer is still always a human decision, by design. We've also identified a real next step -- AI-drafted outreach emails a rep would still review before sending -- as a concrete idea for a future phase, not something we're claiming exists today.

lessons.title: Writing the Model Card and Handoff Docs
lessons.summary: The real model card and handoff documentation for the churn model -- what it predicts, its real ~0.79 AUC, the leakage incident as a documented lesson learned, who owns it, the retrain cadence, and how someone would know if it needs attention.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
A model that only Felix Granger fully understands is a liability the moment he's unavailable -- out sick, on vacation, or simply moved on to the next project. This video writes the document that prevents that: a real model card and handoff doc for the Everpeak churn model, covering what it predicts, its real validated accuracy (~0.79 AUC on an honest, time-consistent backtest), its known limitations -- the leakage incident documented as a lesson learned, not buried -- who owns it day to day, the retrain cadence, and exactly how someone would know if this model needs attention before a renewal decision gets made on a stale or degraded score.

This is the artifact that turns "Felix knows how this works" into something any future data scientist, or Grace Lindqvist on the deployment side, can actually read and act on without a meeting.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a recipe card taped inside a restaurant's kitchen that says not just the dish's name, but how long it actually takes to cook, what ingredient once caused a bad batch and how that got fixed, and who to call if something seems off with tonight's order. A new cook who's never made this dish before can still make it safely and know when to ask for help.

That's what a model card is for Everpeak's churn model. It writes down, in plain language, what the model predicts, how accurate it really is, the one real mistake that happened early on and exactly how it got fixed, who's responsible for keeping it running, how often it gets refreshed, and what someone should watch for if something seems wrong -- so the next person who touches this model doesn't have to start from zero or repeat the same mistake.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A model card earns its place in the handoff only if it's written for someone who wasn't in the room for any of the last eighteen videos -- which means every claim in it has to be specific and checkable, not aspirational. "Predicts churn" is not a model card; "90-day-ahead probability that a given account cancels its subscription, scored weekly for all ~40,000 paying accounts, written to dbo.ChurnRiskScores" is.

The limitations section is the part most model cards get wrong by omission, and it's the part that matters most here specifically because of what already happened. Documenting the leakage incident as a named lesson learned -- `logins_last_30d` and `days_since_last_login` anchored to `ChurnDate` instead of a fixed `OBSERVATION_DATE`, caught via a time-consistent backtest after SHAP flagged those two features as suspiciously dominant -- isn't an embarrassing footnote, it's the single most useful sentence in the document for whoever retrains this model next, because it tells them exactly which mistake not to repeat and exactly what to check for in any new feature before trusting it.

Ownership and retrain cadence need the same specificity: Felix Granger owns the model itself, Grace Lindqvist owns the Azure ML Batch Endpoint deployment it runs on, and retraining happens manually, roughly quarterly, by Felix's team -- not on an automated trigger, which is itself a limitation worth stating plainly rather than implying a cadence more rigorous than what actually exists. The "how would someone know this needs attention" section has to be equally honest: right now, that's a manual check against each quarter's backtest, because there is no automated drift or performance monitoring yet -- a real, named gap, not a hidden one.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- State what the model predicts, specifically

```
MODEL CARD -- EVERPEAK CHURN RISK SCORE

What it predicts: the probability that a given Everpeak account
  cancels its subscription within the next 90 days, as of a weekly
  scoring run.
Scope: all ~40,000 paying accounts, scored every week by an Azure ML
  Batch Endpoint job, written to dbo.ChurnRiskScores (AccountId,
  ScoreDate, ChurnRiskScore, ModelVersion), with a derived RiskTier
  and a SHAP-based plain-language reason in the companion
  dbo.ChurnRiskExplanations table.
Who uses it: Tom Bellamy's Renewals team, as a weekly prioritized
  list with a plain-language reason attached to each flagged account.
```

## Step 2 -- State the real, validated accuracy -- and how it was validated

```
Validated performance: AUC ~0.79, measured via a time-consistent
  backtest -- every historical account scored using only the features
  knowable as of a fixed OBSERVATION_DATE, with nothing derived from
  data after that date. This is the number this model is accountable
  to going forward.

NOT the number: an earlier offline run reported AUC ~0.98. That
  number was invalid due to target leakage (see Known Limitations)
  and should never be cited as this model's accuracy.
```

## Step 3 -- Document the leakage incident as a named lesson learned

```
KNOWN LIMITATIONS -- LESSONS LEARNED

1. TARGET LEAKAGE (found and fixed before production use):
   logins_last_30d and days_since_last_login were originally computed
   using each account's own ChurnDate as the window anchor instead of
   a fixed OBSERVATION_DATE. For a churned account, this measured
   activity in the weeks leading up to churn -- nearly the same
   information as the label itself. SHAP had already flagged these
   two features as dominating nearly every prediction before the
   mechanism was traced; a model leaning that hard on two features is
   itself worth investigating.
   FIX: every trailing-window feature is now computed relative to one
   fixed OBSERVATION_DATE per training row, excluding all later data.
   TAKEAWAY FOR FUTURE WORK: any new trailing-window feature must be
   checked against a fixed observation date before being trusted, and
   SHAP review is now a standing step in every model review cycle.

2. No automated retraining trigger (see Ownership & Cadence below).
3. No automated drift/performance monitoring in production (see
   "How would someone know this needs attention" below).
```

## Step 4 -- State ownership plainly, by name

```
OWNERSHIP
  Model (features, training, validation): Felix Granger, Head of
    Data Science
  Deployment (Azure ML Batch Endpoint, weekly job): Grace Lindqvist,
    ML Engineer
  Data source (EVERPEAK_PROD, source tables): Renata Silva,
    Data/Analytics Engineer
  Consumer / business owner of how the score is used: Tom Bellamy,
    Head of Renewals/Sales; business sponsor: Dana Okafor, VP of
    Customer Success
```

## Step 5 -- State the retrain cadence honestly

```
RETRAIN CADENCE: manual, roughly quarterly, run by Felix Granger's
  team against the latest EVERPEAK_PROD data. There is no automated
  trigger for "the model has gone stale" -- retraining happens on a
  calendar reminder, not a data-driven signal. This is a known
  limitation, not a hidden one.
```

## Step 6 -- Write "how would someone know this needs attention"

```
HOW TO TELL IF THIS MODEL NEEDS ATTENTION (today, honestly manual):
  - Each quarterly retrain includes a fresh time-consistent backtest;
    compare the new AUC against the ~0.79 baseline. A material drop
    is the clearest signal.
  - Watch for a SHAP feature-importance ranking suddenly dominated by
    one or two features, the way the original leakage bug looked --
    that pattern alone is worth a second look before trusting a
    surprising performance jump.
  - Watch for Tom's team reporting that flagged accounts "don't feel
    right" anymore -- a qualitative signal, but a real one, given
    there's no automated drift monitor yet.
  There is currently no automated alert for any of this. Catching a
  real problem between quarterly retrains still depends on someone
  noticing manually -- the same way the original leakage bug was
  caught, which worked, but is not a guarantee against every future
  issue.
```

## Step 7 -- Store it where the next person will actually find it

Save the model card to the team's shared documentation space, link it from the Azure ML Batch Endpoint's own description field, and walk Grace Lindqvist through it directly -- she's the one most likely to be asked "is this still healthy" by someone outside the data science team.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Wrote the model card: predicts 90-day churn probability for ~40,000 accounts, weekly batch scoring to dbo.ChurnRiskScores, real validated AUC ~0.79 via time-consistent backtest (explicitly not the invalid 0.98). Documented the leakage incident -- logins_last_30d/days_since_last_login anchored to ChurnDate instead of OBSERVATION_DATE -- as a named lesson learned with a concrete takeaway for future feature work. Ownership: Felix on the model, Grace on deployment, Renata on the source data. Retrain is manual/quarterly, with no automated drift monitoring -- both stated as real limitations.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Produced the actual handoff documentation for the churn model: what it does, its real accuracy, the one real incident it already survived (documented so it doesn't repeat), who owns each piece, and how someone would currently tell if it needs attention. This is what lets anyone outside Felix's immediate team operate or evaluate this model without a meeting.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've written down, in plain terms, exactly what this model does, how accurate it really is, and what we learned from the one real mistake we caught and fixed early on. It's owned by name, not by assumption, and we're honest that checking its health today is still a manual quarterly process -- a real limitation we're tracking, not hiding.

lessons.title: Wrap-Up: What Shipped, What's Still Manual
lessons.summary: The honest closing assessment of the Everpeak churn-model build -- what's genuinely validated and in use, and what still depends on a human remembering to do it or hasn't been automated yet.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
This is the last video in the series, and like the engagement it closes out, it isn't a highlight reel. Over nineteen lessons, Everpeak Software went from forty thousand paying accounts renewing or churning with no real warning, to a validated, explainable, weekly churn risk score -- built, broken by a real leakage bug, fixed, honestly re-measured at AUC ~0.79, and now genuinely in use by Tom Bellamy's Renewals team every week.

What this video does instead of celebrating is the harder, more useful thing: naming exactly what's still manual, still a human's responsibility, or still not built, so whoever maintains this model next -- possibly Felix Granger's own team, months from now -- isn't caught off guard by a limitation that was always there but never said out loud. Three real gaps get named plainly: no automated retraining trigger, no automated drift or performance monitoring, and no automated retention action. None of them are failures. All three are honest, scoped-out boundaries of what this V1 build was ever meant to cover.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you spent months building a much better smoke detector system for a building -- more sensors, clearer alarms, a system that actually gets tested instead of just trusted. It's genuinely safer than before. But a good contractor doesn't just hand over the keys and call it perfect -- they say the batteries still need someone to check them on a schedule, nothing yet automatically tells you if a sensor's accuracy starts drifting, and if an alarm does go off, a person still has to decide what to actually do about it, because the system doesn't call the fire department on its own.

That's this whole video, for Everpeak's churn model. The model itself is real, it works, and it's genuinely helping the Renewals team today. But retraining it is still a person's job on a calendar reminder, nothing automatically watches whether it's quietly getting worse, and reaching out to a flagged customer is still, and should still be, a human decision.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A credible project retrospective does two things most wrap-ups skip: it states the real deliverable plainly enough that someone who missed the first nineteen videos could still understand what's running, and it names the actual gaps with the same specificity the earlier lessons used for the leakage incident -- not "there's room for improvement," but named, concrete limitations with a reason. For Everpeak, three are worth stating without softening.

First, retraining is manual and calendar-driven, not trigger-driven: Felix Granger's team retrains roughly quarterly, and nothing in the system itself detects that the model has gone stale between those cycles -- a real account-behavior shift could outpace a quarterly schedule and nobody would be automatically told. Second, there's no automated drift or performance monitoring in production: the only way the team currently catches a real-world accuracy problem is the same manual, after-the-fact comparison that caught the original leakage bug -- which worked, but worked because someone happened to look, not because anything was watching continuously. Third, the risk score and its SHAP explanation are surfaced to Tom Bellamy's team, but any actual outreach to a flagged account is still a human email or phone call; nothing in this system drafts, schedules, or sends anything on its own, and that's a deliberate V1 boundary worth restating here, not an oversight.

Naming these is not an admission of failure; overselling completeness after a team already lived through one leakage incident would itself be the kind of trust problem that incident already taught this room to take seriously. The honest version of done is: this solved the specific, real problem it was scoped to solve, these are its real edges, and here's what comes next -- starting with the generative-AI-drafted-outreach idea named honestly in the previous lesson as a concrete, not-yet-built V2 concept, not a feature already live.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- State the finished deliverable in one pass, end to end

```
ORIGIN:          ~40,000 paying accounts renewing annually with no
                 systematic early-warning signal for Tom Bellamy's
                 Renewals team -- churn risk was gut feeling, not data
MODEL V1:        LightGBM, 90-day-ahead churn probability, trained on
                 SQL Server (EVERPEAK_PROD) features: usage, support
                 tickets, invoices, subscription history
INCIDENT FOUND & FIXED: logins_last_30d and days_since_last_login
                 anchored to each account's own ChurnDate instead of
                 a fixed OBSERVATION_DATE -- an offline AUC of ~0.98
                 that didn't hold up in a time-consistent backtest
                 (~0.74 for the original model). Fixed by anchoring
                 every trailing-window feature to one fixed
                 OBSERVATION_DATE per training row.
VALIDATED RESULT: AUC ~0.79 -- the real, standing number, confirmed
                 with explainability (SHAP) and presented to
                 leadership honestly, leakage included
DEPLOYMENT:      Azure ML Batch Endpoint, weekly scoring job, output
                 to dbo.ChurnRiskScores (AccountId, ScoreDate,
                 ChurnRiskScore, ModelVersion), with a derived
                 RiskTier and a SHAP-based plain-language explanation
                 in the companion dbo.ChurnRiskExplanations table
IN REAL USE:     Tom Bellamy's Renewals team works a weekly
                 prioritized list with a reason attached to every
                 flagged account; every outreach decision stays human
DOCUMENTATION:   A model card naming the leakage incident as a lesson
                 learned, ownership by name (Felix Granger / Grace
                 Lindqvist / Renata Silva), and an honest retrain
                 cadence and health-check process
```

Every line above was built, tested, and is genuinely running today -- that's the real, defensible claim this project gets to make.

## Step 2 -- Name what's still manual or unbuilt, specifically

```
GAP 1: No automated retraining trigger. Felix Granger's team retrains
  roughly quarterly, by hand, against fresh EVERPEAK_PROD data. There
  is no signal in the system itself that says "this model has gone
  stale" between those cycles.

GAP 2: No automated data-drift or model-performance monitoring in
  production. The team would currently catch a real-world accuracy
  problem the same way they caught the original leakage bug: manually,
  after the fact, by someone deciding to look -- not because anything
  is watching continuously.

GAP 3: No automated retention action. The risk score and its SHAP
  explanation reach Tom Bellamy's team every week, but any outreach
  to a flagged account -- an email, a call -- is still a human
  decision made by a human rep, never triggered automatically.
```

## Step 3 -- Write the honest one-paragraph summary for whoever reads this next

```
This project replaced a Renewals team working entirely on instinct
with a validated, explainable, weekly churn risk score for all of
Everpeak's paying accounts. It found and fixed a real target-leakage
bug before that bug ever reached a real renewal decision, and it
left behind a model card that documents exactly how that happened so
nobody repeats it. It did not build automated retraining, automated
drift monitoring, or automated retention outreach -- those are real,
named gaps for a future phase, not oversights pretending not to exist.
```

## Step 4 -- Leave a short, prioritized list for a future phase

```
1. Automated performance/drift monitoring in production -- compare
   live batch-scoring outcomes against the validated baseline on a
   schedule, and alert the team automatically. Closes Gap 2 -- the
   single highest-value item, because it's the one failure mode that
   would otherwise only be caught the same slow, manual way the
   original leakage bug was.
2. A trigger-based retrain policy (e.g., retrain automatically once
   drift crosses a threshold, not just once a quarter regardless of
   whether anything changed). Closes Gap 1.
3. Scope the generative-AI-drafted-outreach idea named in the previous
   lesson: an LLM drafting a SHAP-grounded outreach email for a human
   rep to review and edit, never auto-sent. Closes part of Gap 3,
   deliberately keeping a human in the loop on anything that reaches
   a customer.
```

## Step 5 -- Close the series the way it should close: honestly, not triumphantly

This is the last video of twenty. Resist the pull to end on an unqualified victory lap. The real ending is: Everpeak went from no systematic warning at all to a validated, explainable, weekly-refreshed risk score that a real team uses every week to decide who to call first and why -- and one real mistake was found and fixed along the way, which is a better outcome than a project that never finds out its mistakes exist. Three honest, specific limitations remain, named and handed off instead of hidden. That's a finished project, not a perfect one -- and that's the whole point of telling it this way.

Named three real gaps rather than glossing over them: no automated retrain trigger, no automated drift/performance monitoring, and no automated retention action -- outreach stays a human email or call.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Wrapped the project with an honest accounting of what shipped versus what's still open. The validated model, its weekly deployment, and its real use by Tom's team are genuinely done -- that part is real. We also have a short, prioritized list for a future phase, led by automated performance monitoring, so nothing gets rediscovered as a surprise later.
workplaceExplanation.executive: What we built is real: a validated churn model that survived finding and fixing its own mistake, is explainable, and is actually guiding renewal conversations today. We're also telling you plainly what this doesn't cover yet -- retraining is still manual, nothing automatically watches for the model going stale, and reaching out to a customer is still, by design, always a human decision. That's the honest finish line, not an oversold one.
